texts.title: Goblin Market
texts.author: Christina Rossetti
texts.source: From “Goblin Market” in Poems by Christina Rossetti. Text from Project Gutenberg eBook #19188. Public domain in the UK. Long dashes are shown as short dashes.
lines: Morning and evening
Maids heard the goblins cry:
“Come buy our orchard fruits,
Come buy, come buy:
Apples and quinces,
Lemons and oranges,
Plump unpecked cherries,
Melons and raspberries,
Bloom-down-cheeked peaches,
Swart-headed mulberries,
Wild free-born cranberries,
Crab-apples, dewberries,
Pine-apples, blackberries,
Apricots, strawberries;
All ripe together
In summer weather,
Morns that pass by,
Fair eves that fly;
Come buy, come buy:
Our grapes fresh from the vine,
Pomegranates full and fine,
Dates and sharp bullaces,
Rare pears and greengages,
Damsons and bilberries,
Taste them and try:
Currants and gooseberries,
Bright-fire-like barberries,
Figs to fill your mouth,
Citrons from the South,
Sweet to tongue and sound to eye;
Come buy, come buy.”
Evening by evening
Among the brookside rushes,
Laura bowed her head to hear,
Lizzie veiled her blushes:
Crouching close together
In the cooling weather,
With clasping arms and cautioning lips,
With tingling cheeks and finger-tips.
“Lie close,” Laura said,
Pricking up her golden head:
“We must not look at goblin men,
We must not buy their fruits:
Who knows upon what soil they fed
Their hungry thirsty roots?”
“Come buy,” call the goblins
Hobbling down the glen.
“O,” cried Lizzie, “Laura, Laura,
You should not peep at goblin men.”
Lizzie covered up her eyes,
Covered close lest they should look;
Laura reared her glossy head,
And whispered like the restless brook:
“Look, Lizzie, look, Lizzie,
Down the glen tramp little men.
One hauls a basket,
One bears a plate,
One lugs a golden dish
Of many pounds’ weight.
How fair the vine must grow
Whose grapes are so luscious;
How warm the wind must blow
Through those fruit bushes.”
“No,” said Lizzie, “no, no, no;
Their offers should not charm us,
Their evil gifts would harm us.”
She thrust a dimpled finger
In each ear, shut eyes and ran:
Curious Laura chose to linger
Wondering at each merchant man.

texts.title: A Christmas Carol
texts.author: Charles Dickens
texts.source: From A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens (1843), Stave One. Text from Project Gutenberg eBook #46. Public domain in the UK. Long dashes are shown as short dashes.
lines: Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grind-stone, Scrooge! a squeezing,
wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner! Hard and sharp as flint,
from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and
solitary as an oyster. The cold within him froze his old features, nipped his pointed
nose, shrivelled his cheek, stiffened his gait; made his eyes red, his thin lips blue; and
spoke out shrewdly in his grating voice. A frosty rime was on his head, and on his
eyebrows, and his wiry chin. He carried his own low temperature always about with
him; he iced his office in the dog-days; and didn’t thaw it one degree at Christmas.
External heat and cold had little influence on Scrooge. No warmth could warm, no
wintry weather chill him. No wind that blew was bitterer than he, no falling snow was
more intent upon its purpose, no pelting rain less open to entreaty. Foul weather didn’t
know where to have him. The heaviest rain, and snow, and hail, and sleet, could boast
of the advantage over him in only one respect. They often “came down” handsomely,
and Scrooge never did.
Nobody ever stopped him in the street to say, with gladsome looks, “My dear
Scrooge, how are you? When will you come to see me?” No beggars implored him to
bestow a trifle, no children asked him what it was o’clock, no man or woman ever once
in all his life inquired the way to such and such a place, of Scrooge. Even the blind men’s
dogs appeared to know him; and when they saw him coming on, would tug their owners
into doorways and up courts; and then would wag their tails as though they said, “No
eye at all is better than an evil eye, dark master!”
But what did Scrooge care! It was the very thing he liked. To edge his way along the
crowded paths of life, warning all human sympathy to keep its distance, was what the
knowing ones call “nuts” to Scrooge.
Once upon a time – of all the good days in the year, on Christmas Eve – old Scrooge sat
busy in his counting-house. It was cold, bleak, biting weather: foggy withal: and he could
hear the people in the court outside, go wheezing up and down, beating their hands upon
their breasts, and stamping their feet upon the pavement stones to warm them. The city
clocks had only just gone three, but it was quite dark already – it had not been light all day –
and candles were flaring in the windows of the neighbouring offices, like ruddy smears upon
the palpable brown air. The fog came pouring in at every chink and keyhole, and was so
dense without, that although the court was of the narrowest, the houses opposite were
mere phantoms. To see the dingy cloud come drooping down, obscuring everything, one
might have thought that Nature lived hard by, and was brewing on a large scale.
The door of Scrooge’s counting-house was open that he might keep his eye upon his clerk,
who in a dismal little cell beyond, a sort of tank, was copying letters. Scrooge had a very
small fire, but the clerk’s fire was so very much smaller that it looked like one coal. But he
couldn’t replenish it, for Scrooge kept the coal-box in his own room; and so surely as the
clerk came in with the shovel, the master predicted that it would be necessary for them to
part. Wherefore the clerk put on his white comforter, and tried to warm himself at the
candle; in which effort, not being a man of a strong imagination, he failed.
“A merry Christmas, uncle! God save you!” cried a cheerful voice. It was the voice of
Scrooge’s nephew, who came upon him so quickly that this was the first intimation he had of
his approach.
“Bah!” said Scrooge, “Humbug!”
He had so heated himself with rapid walking in the fog and frost, this nephew of
Scrooge’s, that he was all in a glow; his face was ruddy and handsome; his eyes sparkled, and
his breath smoked again.
“Christmas a humbug, uncle!” said Scrooge’s nephew. “You don’t mean that, I am sure?”
“I do,” said Scrooge. “Merry Christmas! What right have you to be merry? What reason
have you to be merry? You’re poor enough.”
“Come, then,” returned the nephew gaily. “What right have you to be dismal? What
reason have you to be morose? You’re rich enough.”
Scrooge having no better answer ready on the spur of the moment, said, “Bah!” again;
and followed it up with “Humbug.”

units.title: Black Beauty
units.summary: When a question gives you line numbers, go back to those lines before you answer. The answer to a retrieval question is usually close by.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 1 to 6. What could the narrator see over the hedge on one side of the meadow?
questions.explanation: Line 3 says that over the hedge on one side “we looked into a ploughed field”. The master’s house was seen over a gate, on the other side.

questions.prompt: Find and copy the word that tells you how many young colts lived in the meadow besides the narrator.
questions.explanation: Line 13 says there were “six young colts in the meadow besides me”.

questions.prompt: “my mother whinnied to me to come” (line 18). What does whinnied mean?
questions.explanation: A whinny is the sound a horse makes. The mother calls her foal over with her voice.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: Line 13 says the colts “were older than I was”, so the first statement is false. Lines 14 to 15 show he ran and galloped with them, so the last one is false too.
questions.misconception: Mixing up older and younger when reading quickly.

statements.s: The other colts were younger than the narrator.
Some of the colts were nearly as large as grown-up horses.
Once the narrator could eat grass, his mother went out to work in the daytime.
The narrator never galloped with the other colts.

questions.prompt: The mother says the colts “have not learned manners” (lines 21 to 22). What does she mean?
questions.explanation: Earlier, line 16 says the colts “would frequently bite and kick”. The mother tells her son never to do this, so bad manners means rough behaviour like biting and kicking.
options: They are not strong enough to work.
They bite and kick when they play.
They do not listen to the master.
They are too young to eat grass.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the text.
questions.explanation: The text moves forward in time: first the foal drinks milk, then he eats grass and his mother works, then the rough play leads to her advice.
items: The narrator lives on his mother’s milk.
His mother starts going out to work in the daytime.
The colts play roughly, with a good deal of kicking.
His mother whinnies to call him over.
She gives him advice about how to behave.

questions.prompt: Why does the mother tell the narrator about his family? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: The mother compares her son with the cart-horse colts. Reminding him of his well-known family is her way of telling him he should behave better than they do. Not enough on its own: a list of the relatives with no reason why she mentions them.
questions.misconception: Retelling what the text says instead of explaining why the character says it.
questions.model: She wants him to know that he comes from a fine family. His father “has a great name” and his grandfather “won the cup”, so she hopes he will live up to them by behaving well and not copying the rough colts.
checklist: Explaining that she wants him to know he comes from a good or famous family (well-bred and well-born, father has a great name, grandfather won the cup, grandmother had a sweet temper).
Linking this to how he should behave: be gentle and good, never learn bad ways, never bite or kick like the cart-horse colts.

questions.prompt: The text begins with a description of the meadow. What is the main effect of starting this way?
questions.explanation: The meadow has clear water, shady trees and a warm shed nearby. Opening with this gentle picture shows the reader the peaceful home the narrator remembers.
options: It shows the calm, safe place where the narrator grew up.
It explains how young horses are trained to work.
It tells the reader that the narrator was unhappy.
It warns the reader that something bad is about to happen.

questions.prompt: Ellie thinks the master did not care much about Duchess. Is she right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Lines 28 to 30 show the opposite of what Ellie thinks. To think a great deal of someone means to respect them, and a pet name is a sign of fondness. Not enough on its own: agreeing with Ellie. Not enough on its own: no on its own, with no evidence.
questions.misconception: Reading ‘thought a great deal of her’ as thinking about her often rather than valuing her.
questions.model: No, Ellie is wrong. The narrator says “our master thought a great deal of her”, which means he valued her highly. He also “often called her Pet”, a fond name that shows he liked her.
checklist: Disagreeing with a reason from the text: the master thought a great deal of her.
Explaining that calling her Pet shows affection or fondness.

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of the narrator’s mother, Duchess? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: An impression is what you think a character is like. Each one needs a quotation or a detail from the text to back it up.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
She is caring, because the foal ran “by her side” in the day and at night he lay “close by her”. She is also wise: the narrator says “I knew she was a wise old horse”, and she gives him sensible advice about how to behave.

Other impressions that count:
Caring or protective: kept him close by her side; he lay close by her at night; they sheltered in the warm shed together
Wise or sensible: “a wise old horse”; gives him advice he has never forgotten
Gentle or well-behaved: “you have never seen me kick or bite”
Strict about manners or wants the best for him: tells him to “never bite or kick even in play”; wants him to grow up gentle and good
Proud of her family: tells him about his father, grandfather and grandmother.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Five Children and It
units.summary: Speech tells you a lot about characters. Look at what they say and also at the words the writer uses to describe how they say it.

questions.prompt: Why was the cave disappointing?
questions.explanation: Line 4 says the cave was disappointing “because there were no shells”.
options: It was too dark to see.
There were no shells in it.
A rat was living in it.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 4 to 7. Find and copy the word that tells you what someone suggested going home for.
questions.explanation: Line 7 says someone had suggested going home for lemonade, because the sand made them thirsty.

questions.prompt: “But Cyril merely observed that his sister must have gone off her nut” (line 24). Which word is closest in meaning to observed here?
questions.explanation: Here observed means said or remarked. Cyril is making a comment about his sister, not looking at something.
questions.misconception: Choosing the most common meaning of observed (watched) without checking how it is used in the sentence.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: Cyril says “I’m not afraid of snakes” (line 13), and Robert says “No, you won’t” when Cyril talks about keeping one (line 16).

statements.s: Cyril said he was afraid of snakes.
The creature was yawning when it came out of the sand.
Robert was happy for Cyril to keep a snake.
Jane asked whether they should take the creature home.

questions.prompt: “their hearts jumped nearly as fast as they did” (lines 32 to 33). What does this tell you about the children?
questions.explanation: The children jump back when the husky voice speaks, and their hearts jump too. This shows they have had a sudden shock.
options: They were excited about going home.

questions.prompt: Match each child to something they say in the text.
questions.explanation: Check the words straight after each piece of speech, such as said Robert bravely (line 36) and Jane said (line 47).

questions.prompt: The creature says “you talk as if I were nobody in particular” (lines 53 to 54). What does this show about how the creature sees itself? Explain your answer.
questions.explanation: Nobody in particular means an ordinary nobody. The creature is offended because it expects to be treated as somebody important. Not enough on its own: it is frightened (it is angry at the idea that it might be).
questions.misconception: Thinking the creature is frightened because Anthea tells it not to be.
questions.model: It shows the creature thinks it is very important and special. It is insulted that the children talk to it like an ordinary animal that might be frightened, and later it cannot believe they do not know what a Psammead is.
checklist: Saying the creature thinks it is important, special or grand.
Explaining why: it is insulted that the children think it could be frightened or hurt, or it is amazed they do not recognise a Psammead.

questions.prompt: “the sand stirred and spun and scattered” (lines 38 to 39). What effect do these words create?
questions.explanation: The writer uses 3 movement verbs joined by and, all starting with s. They make the sand seem to fly about quickly as the creature comes out.
options: They show the creature bursting out in a sudden rush of movement.
They show the children digging slowly and carefully.
They show the weather getting worse.
They show that the sand was wet and heavy.

questions.prompt: Anthea says “I wish you’d come out” and the creature answers “if that’s your wish”. What do you think might happen later in the story? Use evidence from the text to support your prediction.
questions.explanation: A good prediction is based on clues. The creature obeys a wish and is a kind of fairy, which points towards wishes coming true. Not enough on its own: a prediction with no link to the text, such as they will find treasure.
questions.model: I think the creature will grant the children wishes. When Anthea wishes it would come out, it says “if that’s your wish” and does exactly that. It also calls itself a Sand-fairy, and fairies in stories often grant wishes.
checklist: A sensible prediction, such as the creature will grant the children wishes.
Evidence: it comes out when Anthea wishes it would; it says “if that’s your wish”; it is a Sand-fairy.

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of the creature? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Look at what the creature says and how the writer describes it. Each impression needs a detail from the text to support it.
questions.misconception: Describing what the creature looks like instead of what it is like.
questions.model:
The creature is rude, because it says Jane’s hat is “rubbish on her head”. It is also proud: it is offended that the children talk “as if I were nobody in particular”.

Other impressions that count:
Rude or insulting: asks if Jane always talks nonsense; calls her hat rubbish; looks scornfully at the hat
Proud or self-important: “nobody in particular”; amazed they do not know a Psammead
Bad-tempered or easily annoyed: its fur stood out like a cat’s going to fight; it speaks sharply
Sleepy: yawning and rubbing its eyes; thinks it has dropped asleep
Old or out of touch: “I knew the world had changed”.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Life in the Layers
units.summary: Information texts are packed with facts and numbers. Read the question carefully so that you pick the exact fact it asks for.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest tropical rainforest?
questions.explanation: Line 5 says the largest tropical rainforest is the Amazon.

questions.prompt: Find and copy the name of 1 kind of tree that is cut down for its valuable wood.
questions.explanation: Lines 26 to 27 say trees such as mahogany are cut down for their valuable wood.

questions.prompt: “microorganisms break this material down” (line 24). What does break this material down mean here?
questions.explanation: The material is dead leaves, plants and animals. The microorganisms make it rot so it can be used again by the forest.
options: carry it up to the canopy
rot it away into tiny pieces

questions.prompt: Match each layer of the rainforest to its description.
questions.explanation: The layers are described from the top down in lines 12 to 24.
pairs: giant trees in full sunlight and strong winds
a thick green roof of leaves
dark and humid, with plants that have large leaves
gets less than 2% of the sunlight

questions.prompt: Epiphytes grow on trees but they “do not feed on the trees” (line 17). What can you work out about epiphytes?
questions.explanation: Epiphytes take water and nutrients from the air instead of from the tree, so the tree is not harmed by them.
options: They do not harm the trees they grow on.
They only grow on the forest floor.
They kill the trees they grow on.
They need no water to live.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: The UK had around 1,242 millimetres of rain in 2024, much less than 2,000. Rainforests grow around the middle of the Earth, between the tropics.

statements.s: The UK gets more rain each year than a tropical rainforest.
The Amazon covers more than 6 million square kilometres.
The canopy blocks around 95% of the sunlight.
Tropical rainforests grow near the North and South Poles.

questions.prompt: The writer mentions the UK (line 3) and Belgium (line 29). Why do you think the writer compares the rainforest facts with these places? Explain 1 example.
questions.explanation: Writers of information texts often compare a new fact with something familiar so that readers can grasp how big or small it is. Not enough on its own: because the rainforest is in the UK or in Belgium.
questions.model: The numbers are so big that they are hard to picture. Comparing them with places the reader knows helps: the world lost an area of rainforest “about twice the size of Belgium” in 2024, which shows how huge the loss was.
checklist: Explaining that the comparisons help the reader understand or picture big numbers.
A clear example: rainforests get far more rain than the UK, so they are much wetter; or the lost area is twice the size of Belgium, so the loss is enormous.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best sums up lines 25 to 29?
questions.explanation: These lines give several reasons people clear rainforests and then a figure for how much was lost in 2024. The other options are not in the text, or only give part of the picture.
options: People are destroying rainforests, and a huge area was lost in 2024.
Most of the world’s rainforests have now been cleared.
Rainforests grow back quickly after they are cleared.
Farming is the only reason rainforests are disappearing.

questions.prompt: Kofi says the forest floor must be empty of life because it is so dark. Is Kofi right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: The forest floor is dark, but lines 22 to 24 show it is busy with living things that recycle what falls from above. Not enough on its own: yes, because it is dark. Not enough on its own: animals such as spider monkeys (these live in the canopy).
questions.misconception: Assuming that no light means no life.
questions.model: No. Even though the forest floor gets less than 2% of the sunlight, tiny living things called microorganisms live there. They break down fallen leaves and dead animals so the material can be used again by the forest.
checklist: Disagreeing and naming life on the forest floor: microorganisms.
Explaining what they do: break down fallen leaves, dead plants and dead animals so the forest can use the material again.

questions.prompt: How does the text show that rainforests are important but in danger? Give 2 points, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Look across the whole text: the early part shows how rich the rainforest is, and the end shows the threat to it.
questions.model:
Rainforests are important because the Amazon is “home to 10% of the world’s known plant and animal species”. They are in danger because “Rainforests are disappearing quickly” and 67,000 square kilometres were lost in 2024.

Other points that count:
Important: home to 10% of known species; new species still being discovered; each layer is home to different life; material is recycled by the forest
In danger: disappearing quickly; huge areas cleared for farming; trees cut down for wood; roads, dams and mines break the forest up; 67,000 square kilometres lost in 2024.
checklist: Gives 1 point, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different point
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The Railway Children
units.summary: When a question asks why a character acts in a certain way, look at what is happening around them at that moment in the story.

questions.prompt: Where did the rock and trees fall?
questions.explanation: Line 7 says the rock and trees fell on the line with a blundering crash.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 29 to 45. Find and copy the word that tells you what the petticoats were made of.
questions.explanation: Line 32 and line 45 both call them flannel petticoats.

questions.prompt: “Phyllis faltered” (line 40). What does faltered mean?
questions.explanation: Phyllis stops and repeats herself, “you’re not” twice, which shows she is speaking hesitantly.
options: spoke in an unsure, hesitant way

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: Peter says they could not get up a telegraph post (line 24). Line 37 says Peter led and the girls were not far behind.

statements.s: The children climbed a telegraph post.
2 of the flags were set up in heaps of loose stones.
Peter kept 2 flags for himself.
The girls ran ahead of Peter along the railway.

questions.prompt: Peter says “Shut up,” with brief sternness (line 41). Why does he speak like this?
questions.explanation: The train is due in a few minutes. Peter has no time to discuss whether the petticoats can be torn.
options: There is no time to argue because the train is coming.
He wants Phyllis to go home.
He is angry that the petticoats are red.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the text.
questions.explanation: The events follow the story from the landslide (line 7) to the long wait at the end (lines 61 to 72).
items: The rock and trees fall onto the line.
Peter looks at Mother’s watch and says there is no time.
The girls take off their red petticoats.
The petticoats are torn into 6 flags.
The children wait for the train to appear.

questions.prompt: Why did the children run to “the corner that hid the mound” (lines 37 to 38) before waving their flags? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Lines 37 to 38 describe the straight line of railway. A driver coming round a bend would not see the mound until too late, so the flags had to be seen early. Not enough on its own: to get closer to the station.
questions.misconception: Not using the detail about the straight line of railway.
questions.model: Past the corner, the railway ran in a straight line for half a mile. The driver would be able to see the red flags from a long way off and have time to stop before reaching the corner and the mound hidden behind it.
checklist: Explaining that the driver could see them from far away on the straight line (half a mile without curve or corner).
Explaining that this would give the train time or distance to stop before it reached the hidden mound.

questions.prompt: “the great rock, on the top of which the walking trees were” (line 4). Why does the writer describe the trees as walking?
questions.explanation: The trees are on the sliding rock, so they appear to move forward like walkers. When the rock stops, the trees are “ceasing to walk” (line 5).
options: The children were walking under the trees.
The trees had roots that looked like legs.
The trees seemed to move along as the ground slid.
The wind was blowing the leaves about.

questions.prompt: Sanjay thinks that using the petticoats as flags was Peter’s idea. Is he right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Peter later says “it was my idea to wave something red” (lines 57 to 58). That is true, but the petticoats themselves were Bobbie’s idea. Not enough on its own: yes, because Peter says it was his idea (this is only about waving something red).
questions.misconception: Believing a character’s claim without checking the rest of the text.
questions.model: Only partly. Peter had the idea of waving something red (lines 24 to 25), but it was Bobbie who realised the petticoats were red and said “Let’s take them off” (line 34).
checklist: Saying Peter thought of waving something red.
Saying it was Bobbie who realised the petticoats were red and suggested taking them off.

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of Peter? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Peter acts fast and takes charge. Look at how he talks to his sisters as well as what he does.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
Peter is quick-thinking, because he works out that the 11.29 has not gone by and there will be “a most frightful accident”. He is also rather bossy: he takes “the largest flannel petticoat” and keeps 2 flags for himself.

Other impressions that count:
Sensible or quick-thinking: realises the train is due; checks the watch; knows there is no time to run 2 miles; thinks of waving something red
A leader: Peter led the run; tells the others what to do with the flags and sticks
Bossy or wants credit: “Shut up”; takes the largest petticoat; keeps the other 2 flags because it was his idea; the heroic attitude
Frightened but brave: hardly any voice; face whiter than ever, but he still acts.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The Wind in the Willows
units.summary: A character’s feelings can change during a text. Track how they feel at the start and how they feel later, and find a clue for each.

questions.prompt: What had the Mole been doing all morning?
questions.explanation: Line 1 says the Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 7 to 8. Find and copy 1 thing the Mole said when he flung down his brush.
questions.explanation: The Mole said “Bother!” and “O blow!” and also “Hang spring-cleaning!”. Any 1 of these is correct.

questions.prompt: “soft breezes caressed his heated brow” (line 17). What does caressed mean?
questions.explanation: The breezes are soft, so they touch the Mole’s hot forehead gently and kindly.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: The Mole left “without even waiting to put on his coat” (lines 8 to 9), and the rabbit is described as “an elderly rabbit” (line 22).

statements.s: The Mole put on his coat before he left the house.
The Mole came out in a great meadow.
The rabbit at the gap was a young rabbit.
The Mole knocked the rabbit over.

questions.prompt: “Something up above was calling him imperiously” (line 9). What was calling the Mole?
questions.explanation: Lines 4 to 6 say spring was moving in the air above and filling his house with longing. The Mole cannot resist it, so the spring is what calls him.
questions.misconception: Choosing something mentioned later in the text instead of using the clue earlier on.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the text.
questions.explanation: The Mole goes from cleaning (line 1) to digging (lines 11 to 14), then the meadow (line 15) and finally the rabbits at the hedge (lines 22 to 23).
items: The Mole works hard at his cleaning.
He flings down his brush.
He digs up through his tunnel.
He rolls in the warm grass of a meadow.
He bowls over the elderly rabbit.

questions.prompt: “the carol of happy birds fell on his dulled hearing almost like a shout” (lines 18 to 19). Why did the birdsong seem so loud to the Mole? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Line 17 mentions “the seclusion of” his home. Being shut away from the world explains why his hearing was dulled. Not enough on its own: the birds were shouting at him.
questions.misconception: Taking the comparison literally and thinking the birds really shouted.
questions.model: The Mole had lived underground in “the cellarage” for so long that his hearing was used to quiet. After being shut away, even gentle birdsong sounded as loud as a shout.
checklist: Saying he had been underground, shut away, or in the cellarage for a long time.
Explaining that this made him unused to noise, so ordinary birdsong sounded very loud.

questions.prompt: “pop! his snout came out into the sunlight” (line 14). Why does the writer use the word pop!?
questions.explanation: Pop! is a short, lively sound word. It shows the Mole bursting out into the light all at once after a long dig.
options: to show that the Mole was talking to himself
to show that the tunnel had fallen in
to show a sudden, happy moment of breaking through
to show that the Mole had hurt his nose

questions.prompt: Compare how the Mole feels in lines 1 to 6 with how he feels in lines 16 to 21. Use evidence from both parts.
questions.explanation: Comparing means saying how something is different in 2 places. The Mole changes from tired and dusty to delighted once he is outside. Not enough on its own: feelings without any evidence from the text.
questions.model: At the start he is worn out and fed up, with “an aching back and weary arms” and dust in his throat. Later he is full of happiness: he says “This is fine!” and jumps about “in the joy of living”.
checklist: How he feels at the start, with evidence: tired, fed up or uncomfortable (aching back, weary arms, dust in his throat and eyes).
How he feels later, with evidence: happy, free or joyful (“This is fine!”, jumping off all 4 legs, the joy of living).

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of the Mole? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: The Mole does a lot in a short time. His actions and the words the writer uses about him both give clues to what he is like.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
The Mole is impulsive, because he suddenly flings down his brush and bolts out “without even waiting to put on his coat”. He is also cheeky, as he bowls the rabbit over and shouts “Onion-sauce!” at the others.

Other impressions that count:
Hard-working: “working very hard all the morning”; aching back and weary arms
Impatient or impulsive: flung down his brush; bolted out without his coat; “the impatient and contemptuous Mole”
Cheeky or rude: bowled the rabbit over; chaffing the other rabbits; remarked jeeringly
Joyful or full of life: “This is fine!”; jumping in the joy of living.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The Viking Raid
units.summary: Information texts about history often contain many dates. Read slowly and match each date to the right event before you answer.

questions.prompt: On what date did Viking raiders attack Lindisfarne?
questions.explanation: Line 15 says Viking raiders attacked Lindisfarne on 8 June 793.

questions.prompt: Find and copy the other name that Lindisfarne is known by.
questions.explanation: Line 16 says Lindisfarne is also known as Holy Island.

questions.prompt: “bands of these seafaring warriors” (line 2). What does seafaring mean?
questions.explanation: Seafaring people spend their lives travelling on the sea. The Vikings sailed to many far-off places.

questions.prompt: Match each date to what happened.
questions.explanation: The dates are in lines 18, 20, 34 and 42. Check each one carefully, because the text has many dates.
pairs: Viking armies were staying in England through the winter
the community of St Cuthbert moved to Durham

questions.prompt: “took these strange sights as signs that disaster was on its way” (line 13). What does this tell you about people in 793?
questions.explanation: People saw whirlwinds, lightning and what they thought were fiery dragons, and believed these meant something bad would happen.
options: They wrote down every storm they saw.
They knew the Vikings were coming.
They believed strange events in the sky could warn them about the future.
They were not frightened of the weather.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: Alcuin was living far away in the kingdom of the Franks (lines 26 to 27), and the Danelaw was in eastern England (line 37).

statements.s: Vikings reached Iceland and Greenland.
Alcuin was living in Northumbria when he heard about the raid.
The Danelaw was in the west of England.
Archaeologists dug at Coppergate in York between 1976 and 1981.

questions.prompt: Alcuin “asked whether it was a punishment for the sins of the people who lived there” (lines 31 to 32). What does this suggest about what Alcuin believed? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Alcuin was a Christian scholar. Lines 30 to 32 show he looked for a religious reason behind the raid. Not enough on its own: he thought the Vikings were being punished.
questions.misconception: Mixing up who might be punished: Alcuin wonders about the people of Lindisfarne, not the Vikings.
questions.model: It suggests Alcuin believed that God allowed disasters to happen for a reason. He thought the raid “could not have happened by chance”, so it might be a punishment because the people had done wrong.
checklist: Explaining that he believed the raid was sent or allowed by God, or happened for a reason.
Evidence or explanation: it “could not have happened by chance”; he thought the people might have sinned or done wrong.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best sums up lines 40 to 47?
questions.explanation: These lines explain that a Christian community survived, later moved to Durham, and went on making stone carvings such as the Domesday stone.
options: Christian life carried on after the raid, and religious carvings were still made.
The Christians on Lindisfarne gave up and left for good.
Durham was attacked by Vikings in 995.
The Vikings carved the Domesday stone in 793.

questions.prompt: The writer includes words written by people who lived at the time, such as Alcuin’s letter. Why?
questions.explanation: Quotations such as “spattered with the blood of the priests of God” let the reader hear the shock of people who lived through it.
options: to give instructions for visiting Lindisfarne
to show how people at the time felt about the raid
to make the text sound funny

questions.prompt: How does the writer show that the raid on Lindisfarne was a terrible event for the people of Northumbria? Give 2 points, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Use both parts of the text: the build-up and the raid itself, and then the reactions to it.
questions.model:
The writer shows it was terrible because the church was “spattered with the blood of the priests of God”. It also shocked people, because it “struck at the sacred heart of the kingdom”.

Other points that count:
Violence and destruction: heathen men miserably destroyed God’s church; blood of the priests; stripped of all its furnishing
It hit a holy place: one of the most important centres of Christianity; St Cuthbert’s church; the sacred heart of the kingdom
People’s reactions: it shocked people far more than earlier attacks; Alcuin was horrified
It came after other bad times: warning signs and a great famine; Worse was still to come.
checklist: Gives 1 point, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different point
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Bedtime Poems
units.summary: When you compare 2 poems, look at who is speaking and what each poem compares bedtime to. Find a line from each poem to support your answer.

questions.prompt: Look at Poem 1 (lines 1 to 48). What did Wynken, Blynken and Nod sail off in?
questions.explanation: Line 2 says they “Sailed off in a wooden shoe”.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 1 to 12. Find and copy the words that tell you what the nets were made of.
questions.explanation: Line 9 says “Nets of silver and gold have we”.

questions.prompt: “Nurse helps me in when I embark” (line 50). What does embark mean?
questions.explanation: To embark is to get on board a ship or boat. The child pretends the bed is a boat.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the poems is true or false.
questions.explanation: The stars cry “Never afeard are we!” (line 20), so they are not afraid. In Poem 2 the child sails “All night” (line 61).

statements.s: In Poem 1, the old moon laughed and sang a song.
In Poem 1, the stars were afraid of the fishermen.
In Poem 2 (lines 49 to 64), the child sometimes takes a slice of wedding-cake to bed.
In Poem 2, the child sails during the daytime.

questions.prompt: “As prudent sailors have to do” (line 58). Why does the child take things to bed?
questions.explanation: Prudent means careful and sensible. Sailors take supplies with them, so the child does the same as part of the game.
options: to give them to friends on shore
to pretend they are a careful sailor taking supplies on a voyage

questions.prompt: Put these events from Poem 1 in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The moon speaks in lines 5 to 6, the stars in lines 19 to 21, and the shoe comes home in lines 27 to 28.
items: The 3 sail off on a river of crystal light.
The old moon asks where they are going.
The stars tell them to cast their nets.
The wooden shoe comes down from the skies.

questions.prompt: Look at Poem 2 (lines 49 to 64). How does the child feel about going to bed? Explain using evidence from the poem.
questions.explanation: The child turns bedtime into a sailing game and always comes safely back, so the poem feels cheerful and secure. Not enough on its own: scared of the dark, unless it is clearly supported (the poem does not show fear).
questions.misconception: Assuming a child in the dark must be frightened.
questions.model: The child feels that bedtime is an exciting adventure, because their bed is “like a little boat” and they “sail away” each night. They also feel safe, as they wake up “Safe in my room” in the morning.
checklist: A feeling with evidence: excited or adventurous (bed is like a little boat; I go on board; sail away).
A second feeling or a development with evidence: calm or safe (Safe in my room; I find my vessel fast; says good-night happily).

questions.prompt: “Sailed on a river of crystal light” (line 3). What picture does this create?
questions.explanation: Crystal sparkles and shines. The poet turns the night sky into a glittering river for the shoe to sail on.
options: a sparkling, shining path through the sky

questions.prompt: Look at who is speaking in each poem. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Poem 2 begins “My bed is like a little boat”, so the child speaks. Poem 1 is told by someone else, who speaks to the child at the end: “So shut your eyes while Mother sings”.
options: Poem 1 is told by the child going to bed.
Poem 2 is told by the child going to bed, who uses the words I and my.
Both poems are told by the old moon.

questions.prompt: How does Poem 1 make bedtime seem magical? Give 2 ways, using evidence from the poem to support each one.
questions.explanation: Look for places where the poet makes ordinary things (the sky, the moon, a bed) into something magical.
questions.model:
The poet turns the night sky into a sea, with “a river of crystal light” and “a sea of dew”. The moon and stars also come alive: “The old moon laughed and sang a song”.

Other ways that count:
The sky becomes a sea: river of crystal light; sea of dew; twinkling foam; misty sea
Things in the sky come alive and talk: the old moon asks a question, laughs and sings; the stars call out to the fishermen
Impossible events: sailing in a wooden shoe; fishing for stars; the shoe coming down from the skies
Words about beauty and wonder: beautiful sea; wonderful sights; beautiful things; so pretty a sail.
checklist: Gives 1 way, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different way
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Rikki-Tikki-Tavi
units.summary: Writers often compare one thing with another to help you picture it. Ask yourself what the 2 things have in common.

questions.prompt: What washed Rikki-tikki out of his burrow?
questions.explanation: Line 11 says a high summer flood washed him out of the burrow.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 6 to 10. Find and copy the word that tells you what colour Rikki-tikki’s eyes were.
questions.explanation: Line 7 says his eyes and the end of his nose were pink.

questions.prompt: “Rikki-tikki liked it immensely” (line 36). What does immensely mean?
questions.explanation: Immensely means hugely or very much. Rikki-tikki really enjoyed the raw meat.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: The big man said he was “not dead but half choked” (line 18). Nag was “five feet long” (line 58).
questions.misconception: Remembering Teddy’s words (a dead mongoose) instead of what the big man said.

statements.s: The big man said the mongoose was dead.
The family wrapped the mongoose in cotton wool.
Rikki-tikki jumped onto Teddy’s shoulder.
Nag was 3 feet long.

questions.prompt: Chuchundra “never comes out into the middle of the floor, but always creeps round by the wall” (lines 3 to 4). What does this suggest about Chuchundra?
questions.explanation: Creeping round the edges instead of crossing the open floor suggests Chuchundra is nervous and keeps out of danger.

questions.prompt: Match each character to what they are.
questions.explanation: Each character is introduced with a description: lines 2, 3, 58 and 27 to 28 tell you who is who.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 1 to 5. How does the opening make the reader want to read on? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: The first lines give a promise of action. This hooks the reader before the story goes back to explain how Rikki-tikki arrived. Not enough on its own: it describes what a mongoose looks like (that comes after the opening).
questions.model: It tells us straight away about “the great war that Rikki-tikki-tavi fought single-handed”. The reader wants to know who he fought and how a small animal could win a war on his own.
checklist: Identifying what the opening tells us: there will be a great war or big fight, which Rikki-tikki fought single-handed.
Explaining the effect: it makes the reader curious or excited to find out who the enemy is and what happens.

questions.prompt: “he stayed balancing to and fro exactly as a dandelion tuft balances in the wind” (lines 59 to 60). What does this comparison show about Nag?
questions.explanation: A dandelion tuft sways gently without falling. Nag holds himself up and sways in the same smooth, controlled way, which makes him seem even more threatening.
questions.misconception: Thinking a comparison means the 2 things are alike in every way (Nag is not fluffy).
options: Nag is being blown away by the wind.
Nag sways smoothly and lightly, ready to strike.

questions.prompt: What do you think will happen between Rikki-tikki and Nag? Use evidence from the text to support your prediction.
questions.explanation: The opening lines already hint at a war, and the end of the extract brings in a dangerous enemy. Put these clues together. Not enough on its own: a prediction with no link to the text.
questions.model: I think Rikki-tikki will fight Nag and win. The story opens by saying it is about “the great war that Rikki-tikki-tavi fought single-handed”, and Nag is cruel because he ate one of Darzee’s babies, so Rikki-tikki has a reason to fight him.
checklist: A sensible prediction, such as they will fight, or Rikki-tikki will defeat Nag.
Evidence: the great war in line 1; Rikki-tikki did the real fighting; his war cry; mongooses hunt snakes; Nag ate a baby bird.

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of Nag in lines 55 to 62? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Nag appears only at the very end, but the writer packs many clues into a few lines. The reactions of other animals are clues too.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
Nag is frightening, because his hiss is “a horrid cold sound” that makes Rikki-tikki jump back. He also seems cruel, with “wicked snake’s eyes”, and Darzee has told us he ate a baby bird.

Other impressions that count:
Frightening or dangerous: the low hiss; Rikki-tikki jumps back 2 clear feet; Darzee and his wife cowered down
Big or powerful: big black cobra; “he was five feet long”; rises up inch by inch with his hood spread
Cruel or wicked: wicked snake’s eyes; he ate one of Darzee’s babies
Cold or hard to read: eyes that never change their expression, whatever he is thinking.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Mountains of Fire
units.summary: Information texts often explain how one thing causes another. Look for linking words such as so, because and when.

questions.prompt: What is the name for melted rock that is still deep underground?
questions.explanation: Lines 2 to 3 say this melted rock is called magma. It is only called lava once it has erupted.
questions.misconception: Mixing up magma (underground) and lava (after it erupts).

questions.prompt: Find and copy the name of the area around the Pacific Ocean where many volcanoes lie.
questions.explanation: Lines 15 to 16 say many volcanoes lie around the Pacific Ocean, in an area known as the Ring of Fire.

questions.prompt: “a broad, gentle slope” (line 12). What does broad mean?
questions.explanation: Shield volcanoes spread out a long way, so their slope is wide rather than steep.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: Europe has 82 volcanoes, and 32 of these are in Iceland (line 16). Mount Fuji is a composite volcano (lines 9 to 10).
questions.misconception: Taking the wrong number from a sentence that contains 2 numbers.

statements.s: There are more than 1,500 active volcanoes on Earth.
Europe has 32 volcanoes.
Mount Fuji is a shield volcano.
Pompeii was destroyed in the year 79 CE.

questions.prompt: “most of the world’s volcanoes are not watched closely at all” (lines 23 to 24). Why could this be dangerous?
questions.explanation: Line 23 explains that scientists study signals so people can be warned. If a volcano is not watched, those signals could be missed.
options: Volcanoes erupt more often when nobody is watching.
The volcanoes would stop being active.
People living nearby might get no warning before an eruption.
Scientists would forget where the volcanoes are.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of an eruption in the order the text explains them.
questions.explanation: Lines 2 to 7 explain the process step by step, from melting rock to lava.
items: Deep underground, some rock gets so hot that it melts.
The magma rises because it is lighter than the rock around it.
The magma forces its way through a weak spot in the crust.
The magma erupts and is now called lava.

questions.prompt: Why do you think the writer gives the example of Montserrat as well as Pompeii? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: The words “Much more recently” (line 20) signal the contrast. Giving examples from very different times shows that the danger has not gone away. Not enough on its own: to show that Pompeii is on Montserrat.
questions.model: Pompeii was destroyed nearly 2,000 years ago, in 79 CE. Montserrat’s eruption began in 1995, “Much more recently”, so the writer shows that volcanoes are still deadly today, not only in ancient times.
checklist: Explaining that Pompeii happened long ago (79 CE, Roman times) and Montserrat happened recently (1995).
Explaining the purpose: to show eruptions are still a danger to people today.

questions.prompt: Shield volcanoes are “shaped like a warrior’s shield” (lines 12 to 13). What does this comparison help the reader to picture?
questions.explanation: A warrior’s shield is broad and gently curved. Shield volcanoes have this low, wide shape because their runny lava spreads out a long way.
options: a tall volcano with a sharp, pointed top
a wide volcano with a low, gently curved shape
a volcano that protects people from lava

questions.prompt: Maya says that a volcano which has been quiet for hundreds of years is safe and will never erupt again. Is she right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Line 18 shows that a long quiet spell is normal for some volcanoes. It does not mean they are finished. Not enough on its own: no, with no evidence.
questions.misconception: Thinking a volcano that has been quiet for a long time can never erupt again.
questions.model: No, Maya is wrong. The text says some volcanoes “stay quiet for tens, hundreds or even thousands of years”. This means a quiet volcano can still erupt one day.
checklist: Disagreeing with Maya.
Using the text: some volcanoes stay quiet for tens, hundreds or even thousands of years (and can then erupt).

questions.prompt: Compare composite volcanoes with shield volcanoes. Explain 2 differences, using evidence from the text.
questions.explanation: A difference needs both sides: say what one type is like and what the other is like. Not enough on its own: facts about only 1 type of volcano with no comparison.
questions.model:
Composite volcanoes are “tall with steep sides”, but shield volcanoes have “a broad, gentle slope”. Composite volcanoes are built from layers of lava, ash and rock, whereas shield volcanoes are made almost entirely of runny lava.

Other differences that count:
Shape: composite volcanoes are tall with steep sides; shield volcanoes are broad with a gentle slope
What they are made of: composite volcanoes have layer upon layer of lava, ash and rock; shield volcanoes are made almost entirely of runny lava
Examples: Mount Fuji in Japan is composite; the Hawaiian Islands are shield volcanoes.
checklist: Gives 1 difference, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different difference
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The Secret Garden
units.summary: Look out for moments when a character’s mood changes. The writer often tells you with a single word or phrase.

questions.prompt: What did Mary find in the newly-turned soil?
questions.explanation: Lines 27 to 28 say it was more than a ring: it was an old key that looked as if it had been buried a long time.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 24 to 28. Find and copy the words that tell you what the key looked like before Mary picked it up.
questions.explanation: Lines 25 to 26 say it was something like a ring of rusty iron or brass.
questions.answer: a ring of rusty iron or brass
accept: ring of rusty iron or brass
something like a ring of rusty iron or brass

questions.prompt: “She was so happy that she scarcely dared to breathe.” (line 17). What does scarcely mean?
questions.explanation: Scarcely means hardly or almost not. Mary keeps very still so that she does not frighten the robin.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: Lines 34 to 35 say Mary was not a child who had been trained to ask permission or consult her elders. Lines 55 to 56 say she could see nothing but ivy leaves.

statements.s: The robin flew up into a tree before Mary picked up the ring.
Mary asked an adult what she should do with the key.
Mary put the key in her pocket.
Mary found the door hidden behind the ivy.

questions.prompt: Mary looked at the key “with an almost frightened face” (line 29). Why?
questions.explanation: Straight afterwards she whispers “Perhaps it is the key to the garden!” (lines 31 to 32). She is overwhelmed by what she might have found.
options: She was scared of the robin.
She thought she would be told off for digging.
She had hurt her finger on the rusty key.
She realised she might have found something very important and secret.

questions.prompt: These events come from both parts of the story. Put them in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The story moves from the robin (lines 5 to 21) to the key (lines 24 to 32) and then to the wall (lines 53 to 56).
items: Mary tells the robin he is prettier than anything else in the world.
The robin hops over a small pile of freshly turned earth.
Mary picks up the ring and sees it is a key.
Mary whispers that it might be the key to the garden.
Mary walks up and down, looking at the ivy on the wall.

questions.prompt: Mary was pleased that “nobody would ever know where she was” (line 42). Why did this idea please her? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Lines 40 to 44 describe what Mary imagines. The thought of a secret place of her own is what pleases her. Not enough on its own: she wanted to hide from the robin.
questions.model: She liked the idea of having a secret place that belonged only to her. She could go in every day, shut the door behind her and play her own games alone, while everyone else thought the door was still locked.
checklist: Saying she wanted a secret or private place of her own.
Explaining with the text: she could go in every day and shut the door; she could make up a play of her own and play it alone; people would think the door was still locked and the key buried.

questions.prompt: “fighting with the wind had stirred her blood” (line 49). What does stirred her blood suggest?
questions.explanation: The fresh moor air had woken Mary up. In India she had been weak and languid, but now she feels lively and wants to do new things.
options: It made her angry with the weather.
It made her feel lively and full of energy.

questions.prompt: Josh says Mary is happy all the way through this text. Is he right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Characters’ feelings change. Lines 56 to 58 show Mary’s mood drops when the ivy hides the door. Not enough on its own: no, with no evidence.
questions.misconception: Judging a character’s feelings from the start of a text only.
questions.model: No. Mary is very happy with the robin, but near the end she is “very much disappointed” because she cannot find the door, and “Something of her contrariness came back to her”.
checklist: Disagreeing with Josh.
Evidence of a different feeling: very much disappointed; her contrariness came back; she thought it seemed so silly; an almost frightened face when she found the key.

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of the robin in lines 1 to 26? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: The writer describes the robin almost as if he were a person. His actions are your best evidence.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
The robin is proud: he “puffed his tiny breast out” and was “so fine and so grand”. He is also clever, because he pretends to peck at the earth “to persuade her that he had not followed her”.

Other impressions that count:
Proud or showing off: puffed his tiny breast out; so fine and so grand; showing how important a robin could be
Clever or sly: pretending to peck things out of the earth to persuade her he had not followed her
Friendly or trusting: he followed her; he allowed her to draw closer and closer; it was as if he were talking
Lively: hopping about; flirted his tail; twittered.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The Village Blacksmith
units.summary: Poems often show a character in different settings. Compare how the person seems in one part of the poem with how they seem in another.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 13 to 18. When can you hear the bellows blow?
questions.explanation: Line 13 says “Week in, week out, from morn till night,” and line 14 says “You can hear his bellows blow”.
options: from morning till night, every week

questions.prompt: Look at lines 25 to 30. Find and copy the words that tell you where the blacksmith’s daughter sings.
questions.explanation: Line 29 says she is singing in the village choir.

questions.prompt: “Toiling, rejoicing, sorrowing” (line 37). What does toiling mean?
questions.explanation: To toil is to work very hard. It sums up the blacksmith’s long days at the forge.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the poem is true or false.
questions.explanation: The children “love to see the flaming forge” (line 21). It is his daughter who sings; his wife has died (line 34).
questions.misconception: Mixing up the daughter and the mother in lines 28 to 31.

statements.s: The blacksmith’s hair is crisp, black and long.
The blacksmith goes to church on Sundays.
The children are frightened of the forge.
The blacksmith’s wife sings in the village choir.

questions.prompt: “His brow is wet with honest sweat” (line 9). What does the word honest suggest?
questions.explanation: His sweat comes from fair, hard work. Lines 10 to 12 add that he earns what he can and owes nothing to anyone.
options: He tells everyone the truth about his sweat.
He sweats because he is nervous.
He earns his living by hard, fair work.
He is too hot to work.

questions.prompt: Match each thing in the poem to what it is compared to.
questions.explanation: Look for the words like and as. The comparisons are in lines 6, 17, 24 and 31.
pairs: a sexton ringing the village bell

questions.prompt: Read lines 39 to 42. What do these lines tell you about why the blacksmith sleeps well at night? Explain using the poem.
questions.explanation: Repose means rest or sleep. The poet links a full day of work with a well-earned night’s sleep. Not enough on its own: he is old and tired, with no link to his work.
questions.model: Every day he starts a task and finishes it by the evening. Because he has worked hard and got something done, he feels he has earned his rest: “Has earned a night’s repose”.
checklist: Explaining that he works hard and completes a task every day (each morning a task begins, each evening it closes; something attempted, something done).
Explaining that he has earned or deserves his rest.

questions.prompt: How are lines 43 to 48 different from the rest of the poem?
questions.explanation: These lines begin “Thanks, thanks to thee, my worthy friend”. The poet turns from describing the blacksmith to thanking him and drawing a lesson about life.
options: The poet speaks directly to the blacksmith and explains the lesson he has taught.
They tell the reader about the blacksmith’s wife.
They describe the chestnut-tree outside the smithy.
They describe the children watching the forge.

questions.prompt: Compare the blacksmith at work (lines 13 to 18) with the blacksmith at church (lines 25 to 36). How is he different? Use evidence from both parts.
questions.explanation: The poem shows 2 sides of the same man: tough at the forge and tender with his family. Not enough on its own: answers that describe only 1 of the 2 parts.
questions.misconception: Describing only 1 side of a comparison.
questions.model: At work he is strong and steady, swinging “his heavy sledge” with “measured beat and slow”. At church he shows his gentle, emotional side: his daughter’s singing “makes his heart rejoice” and he wipes away a tear.
checklist: How he is at work, with evidence: strong, hard-working, steady or noisy (swings his heavy sledge; bellows blow from morn till night).
How he is at church, with evidence: gentle, loving, emotional or sad (heart rejoices; thinks of his wife; wipes a tear).

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of the blacksmith? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the poem to support each one.
questions.explanation: Use the whole poem. Some impressions come from how he looks and some from what he does and feels.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
The blacksmith is very strong: he has “large and sinewy hands” and arms “strong as iron bands”. He is also a loving father, because his daughter’s voice “makes his heart rejoice”.

Other impressions that count:
Strong: a mighty man; large and sinewy hands; brawny arms; strong as iron bands
Hard-working: week in, week out, from morn till night; honest sweat; each morning sees some task begin
Honest or proud: earns whate’er he can; owes not any man; looks the whole world in the face
Loving or emotional: sits among his boys; heart rejoices at his daughter’s voice; wipes a tear thinking of his wife.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The Titanic
units.summary: When an information text gives numbers, check exactly what each number counts before you use it in an answer.

questions.prompt: Where did Titanic set sail from on her first voyage?
questions.explanation: Line 15 says Titanic set sail from Southampton, bound for New York.

questions.prompt: Find and copy the name of the ship that sent the first warning of ice.
questions.explanation: Lines 25 to 26 say the first warning of ice arrived by wireless from another ship, the Caronia.

questions.prompt: “She docked in New York” (lines 38 to 39). What does docked mean?
questions.explanation: A ship docks when it reaches a harbour and is tied up. Carpathia brought the survivors to New York.
options: arrived and tied up in a harbour

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: The ship carried 20 lifeboats (line 22), and the wreck was found on 1 September 1985 (line 44).

statements.s: Titanic had room for 3,320 people.
Titanic carried 30 lifeboats.
Titanic sank on 15 April 1912.
The wreck was found in 1912.

questions.prompt: The crew “had not been prepared for the ship sinking” (lines 30 to 31). What does this help to explain?
questions.explanation: The same sentence goes on to say that in the panic many lifeboats were lowered into the sea before they were full.
options: why the ship hit the iceberg
why the ship used the code SOS
why many lifeboats were lowered before they were full
why the water was so cold

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
questions.explanation: Use the dates and times: 10 April, the morning of 14 April, 23.40, 00.45 and 04.10 on 15 April.
items: Titanic sets sail from Southampton.
A warning of ice arrives from the Caronia.
Titanic strikes an iceberg.
The wireless operators send a call for help.
Carpathia picks up the first lifeboat.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 10 to 12. What false story about Titanic does the writer want to correct, and how does the writer do it?
questions.explanation: Information texts sometimes correct common mistakes. Here the writer uses facts about Titanic’s speed to show the speed-record story is not supported. Not enough on its own: the story that Titanic was unsinkable (that is corrected in lines 19 to 21).
questions.model: Some people say Titanic’s captain was trying to set a speed record. The writer corrects this by explaining that she “was not designed to be the fastest ship on the ocean” and that these stories “have no evidence to support them”.
checklist: Identifying the false story: that the captain was trying to set a speed record.
How the writer corrects it: she was not built to be the fastest ship; her speeds are given; there is no evidence for the stories.

questions.prompt: “somewhere in the dark depths of the North Atlantic” (lines 43 to 44). What feeling does this phrase create?
questions.explanation: The words somewhere and dark depths suggest a deep, hidden place where nobody knew exactly where the wreck lay for more than 70 years.
options: a feeling of speed and rushing
a feeling of mystery, because the wreck was lost and hidden
a feeling of excitement, like a party
a feeling of warmth and comfort

questions.prompt: Lena says that if every lifeboat had been full, everyone on board would have been saved. Is she right? Use numbers from the text to explain.
questions.explanation: About 2,200 people is far more than 1,178 places, so about 1,000 people could never have had a place. Lines 36 to 37 say this directly. Not enough on its own: no, with no numbers or evidence.
questions.misconception: Thinking the only problem was that lifeboats left half empty.
questions.model: No. The lifeboats could hold about 1,178 people, but about 2,200 people were on board. The text says that even if every lifeboat had been filled, “there would have been no place for about 1,000 people”.
checklist: Disagreeing with Lena.
Using the numbers: lifeboats held about 1,178; about 2,200 on board; no place for about 1,000 people; enough for only about half the people on board.

questions.prompt: How does the text show that Titanic was a remarkable ship when she was built? Give 2 points, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Lines 1 to 9 are full of facts showing how special the ship was. Choose 2 different kinds of point, such as size and comfort.
questions.model:
Titanic was huge: she was “the largest object ever to move on water”. She was also very luxurious, with “the first swimming pool ever put on board a ship”.

Other points that count:
Size: the largest object ever to move on water; 852.5 feet long; 10 decks; room for 3,320 people
Luxury: squash courts, a Turkish bath, a gymnasium, a barber’s shop; the first swimming pool on a ship
Even the cheaper cabins were special: third-class cabins were better than those on other liners
Her builders were confident: they claimed she was practically unsinkable.
checklist: Gives 1 point, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different point
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: How the Whale Got His Throat
units.summary: Funny stories still need careful reading. Ask what the writer is doing to make you laugh, and find the words that do it.

questions.prompt: What was the Mariner sitting on when the Whale found him?
questions.explanation: Lines 18 to 20 say the Whale found the Mariner on a raft, in the middle of the sea.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 6 to 7. Find and copy the words the Whale said when he stood up on his tail.
questions.explanation: Line 7 says the Whale stood up on his tail and said he was hungry.

questions.prompt: “he found one single, solitary shipwrecked Mariner” (line 20). What does solitary mean?
questions.explanation: Solitary means on his own. The words single and solitary both stress that there was only 1 Mariner.
questions.misconception: Guessing a feeling word (sad) because being alone at sea sounds unhappy.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: The Whale swam “as fast as he could swim” (lines 17 to 18), and the ’Stute Fish is called “a small ‘Stute Fish” (line 5).

statements.s: The ’Stute Fish said that Man tasted nice but nubbly.
The Whale swam slowly to find the Mariner.
The Mariner had his mummy’s leave to paddle.
The ’Stute Fish was the largest fish in the sea.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 28 to 34. Why did the Whale feel most unhappy?
questions.explanation: The Mariner stumped, jumped, thumped and bumped inside the Whale. All that movement is what made the Whale so uncomfortable.
options: The Mariner was jumping and banging about inside him.
The ’Stute Fish had tricked him into eating fish.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the story.
questions.explanation: The story moves from the Whale’s huge appetite (lines 1 to 4) to the trip (line 17), the swallowing (lines 23 to 26) and the Mariner’s dancing (lines 29 to 33).
items: The Whale eats nearly every fish in the sea.
The ’Stute Fish asks the Whale if he has ever tasted Man.
The Whale swims to “latitude Fifty North, longitude Forty West”.
The Whale swallows the Mariner and his raft.
The Mariner jumps and bangs about inside the Whale.

questions.prompt: The Mariner “had his mummy’s leave to paddle” (line 21). Why is this detail funny? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Much of the humour in this story comes from silly details told as if they were serious, like a shipwrecked sailor asking his mummy’s permission. Not enough on its own: because paddling is dangerous.
questions.model: It is funny because the Mariner is a grown man who has been shipwrecked in the middle of the sea, yet he still asks his mother before paddling his toes. The storyteller says he would never have done it without permission, because he was so sensible.
checklist: Explaining the joke: a grown-up sailor, alone and shipwrecked, would not need his mother’s permission to paddle.
Linking it to the text: he is a man of infinite-resource-and-sagacity, so he is so sensible and well-behaved that he would not paddle without leave.

questions.prompt: Lines 29 to 33 are full of rhyming pairs, such as “he stumped and he jumped” (line 29). What effect does this have?
questions.explanation: The long list of rhyming actions is fun to read aloud and seems never to end, just as the Mariner never stops moving inside the Whale.
options: It makes his movements sound wild, noisy and funny, and shows they went on and on.
It makes the Mariner seem calm and still.
It makes the story feel sad and serious.
It shows that the Mariner had fallen asleep.

questions.prompt: The ’Stute Fish calls the Whale “Noble and generous Cetacean” (lines 7 to 8). Why do you think the fish speaks to him like this? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: ’Stute means clever. The fish chooses polite, grand words on purpose, at a very dangerous moment. Not enough on its own: because the Whale really is noble and generous (he has just eaten every fish).
questions.model: The ’Stute Fish is the last fish left in the sea and the Whale has just said he is hungry. By flattering the Whale with grand words, the clever fish keeps him in a good mood and gets him interested in eating Man instead.
checklist: Explaining that the fish is flattering the Whale or trying to please him.
Explaining why: the Whale is hungry and the fish is the last one left, so it wants to save itself or steer the Whale towards Man.

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of the Mariner? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: The storyteller tells us about the Mariner directly and also shows us what he does once he is swallowed.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
The Mariner is clever, because he is described as “a man of infinite-resource-and-sagacity”. He also fights back, as he stumps, thumps and bangs about inside the Whale until the Whale feels “most unhappy indeed”.

Other impressions that count:
Clever or resourceful: a man of infinite-resource-and-sagacity (repeated several times)
Well-behaved or obedient: he had his mummy’s leave to paddle
Not easily beaten or determined: he jumps, bangs and bites inside the Whale and makes it most unhappy
Calm or relaxed: trailing his toes in the water while shipwrecked.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Treasure Island
units.summary: Stories told by a narrator looking back can show how the narrator felt at the time. Look for words such as I remember and for the narrator’s own feelings.

questions.prompt: What did the captain ask for when Jim’s father came to the door?
questions.explanation: Line 10 says that when Jim’s father appeared, the captain called roughly for a glass of rum.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 30 to 31. Find and copy the words that tell you what the captain took with him when he went to the cove or the cliffs.
questions.explanation: Lines 30 to 31 say he hung round the cove or upon the cliffs with a brass telescope.

questions.prompt: “he drank slowly, like a connoisseur” (line 11). What is a connoisseur?
questions.explanation: A connoisseur is an expert who enjoys good things. The captain drinks slowly, “lingering on the taste”.
options: someone who is in a great hurry
someone who knows a lot about something and enjoys it

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: Jim’s father said there was very little company (line 15). The captain promised a fourpenny “on the first of every month” (lines 42 to 43).

statements.s: The captain threw down 3 or 4 gold pieces.
Jim’s father said the inn had plenty of company.
The captain was set down at the Royal George the morning before he arrived.
The captain promised to pay Jim every week.

questions.prompt: People at the inn “soon learned to let him be” (line 34). What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: The captain would not answer when spoken to and looked up fierce. People quickly worked out that it was best not to bother him.
options: They did not notice he was there.
They found him unfriendly, so they left him alone.
They liked talking to him every evening.
They were cross that he paid in gold.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the description of the captain to the comparison the writer uses.
questions.explanation: The comparisons are in lines 8 to 9, line 33, line 40 and lines 21 to 22.
pairs: tuned and broken at the capstan bars
the noise he made through his nose
how quiet he was when a seaman was present
how he looked when he threw down the gold

questions.prompt: Jim says “I paid pretty dear for my monthly fourpenny piece” (line 55). What does he mean? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: To pay dear for something is to suffer for it. Lines 49 to 56 show what Jim suffered. Not enough on its own: jim had to pay the captain money.
questions.misconception: Reading paid literally, as if Jim handed over money.
questions.model: Jim means the coin cost him far more than it was worth, but not in money. Watching for the one-legged man gave him terrible nightmares in which the man would “leap and run and pursue” him.
checklist: Explaining that he paid in a different way, not with money: the job cost him a lot in fear.
Using the text: the seafaring man with one leg haunted his dreams; he saw him in “in a thousand forms”; it was the worst of nightmares; abominable fancies.

questions.prompt: “when the wind shook the four corners of the house and the surf roared along the cove” (line 50). Why does the writer describe the storm here?
questions.explanation: The shaking house and roaring sea make the night feel wild and scary, which builds up the fear in Jim’s dreams about the one-legged man.
options: to create a frightening mood that matches Jim’s nightmares
to explain why the captain left the inn
to show that it was summer
to show that Jim enjoyed stormy weather

questions.prompt: Do you think the seafaring man with one leg will come to the Admiral Benbow? Use evidence from the text to support your prediction.
questions.explanation: Use what the captain does and fears as clues. Writers often prepare readers for a character who will turn up later. Not enough on its own: a prediction with no link to the text.
questions.model:
Yes, I think he will come. The captain is clearly expecting him: he asks every day if any seafaring men have gone by and pays Jim to keep his “weather-eye open” for him. The writer would not build up this fear unless the man was going to appear.

Also fine: a No prediction if it is supported, for example the inn is lonely and the captain hides well.
checklist: A clear prediction.
Evidence: the captain watches with a telescope; asks every day about seafaring men; pays Jim to look out for the man; chose a lonely inn; looks through the curtain at every seaman.

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of Jim, the narrator? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Jim is the narrator, so his impressions come from how he tells the story as well as from what he does.
