questions.misconception: Writing about the captain instead of Jim.
questions.model:
Jim is observant, because he remembers the captain’s “black, broken nails” and the scar on his cheek in great detail. He is also easily frightened at night: the one-legged man “haunted my dreams”.

Other impressions that count:
Observant or has a good memory: I remember him as if it were yesterday; detailed description of the captain’s clothes, hands and scar
Frightened or imaginative: the man haunted his dreams; “a thousand diabolical expressions”; the worst of nightmares
Loyal or helpful: a sharer in his alarms; keeps watch for the captain
Bold: still asks the captain for his wage even when he is stared down.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The Walrus and the Carpenter
units.summary: Nonsense poems are meant to be silly, but questions about them still need evidence. Point to the exact line that makes something funny or odd.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 7 to 12. How was the moon shining?
questions.explanation: Line 7 says “The moon was shining sulkily”.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 13 to 18. Find and copy the words that explain why no birds were flying overhead.
questions.explanation: Line 18 gives the silly reason: there were no birds to fly.
questions.answer: There were no birds to fly

questions.prompt: “They wept like anything to see” (line 21). What does wept mean?
questions.explanation: To weep is to cry. Later the Carpenter “shed a bitter tear” (line 30).

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the poem is true or false.
questions.explanation: Line 16 says no cloud was in the sky. When asked about the maids, the Carpenter says “I doubt it” (line 29).

statements.s: The moon thought it was rude of the sun to be shining.
There were many clouds in the sky.
The Walrus imagined maids with mops sweeping for half a year.
The Carpenter believed the maids could clear the sand.

questions.prompt: The Carpenter “shed a bitter tear” (line 30). What does this suggest about him?
questions.explanation: The Carpenter has just said he doubts the sand could ever be cleared. A bitter tear shows he feels sorry and gloomy about it.
options: He had sand in his eyes.
He was pleased with the Walrus’s idea.
He was gloomy because he thought the sand could never be cleared.

questions.prompt: Put these events from the poem in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The poem moves from the sky (lines 1 to 12) to the beach (lines 13 to 30) and then to the Oysters (lines 31 to 54).
items: The sun shines in the middle of the night.
The moon complains that the sun has come to spoil the fun.
The Walrus and the Carpenter weep at all the sand.
The Walrus invites the Oysters to walk with them.
The young Oysters hurry up, eager for the treat.

questions.prompt: Lines 13 to 18 state things that are very obvious, such as “The sea was wet as wet could be” (line 13). Why do you think the poet does this? Explain using the poem.
questions.explanation: Nonsense poets often make jokes by stating the obvious as if it were surprising news. Not enough on its own: to describe the weather at the beach.
questions.misconception: Treating nonsense lines as serious description.
questions.model: The poet does it to be funny. Everyone knows the sea is wet, so saying it so seriously is silly. The joke carries on in line 15, “You could not see a cloud, because”, and line 16, “No cloud was in the sky”, which explain something that needs no explaining.
checklist: Explaining that it is meant to be funny or silly, because it is a nonsense poem.
Explaining how: the statements are obviously true or explain themselves (the sea is wet; the sands are dry; no cloud because no cloud in the sky; no birds because there were no birds).

questions.prompt: The Walrus promises “A pleasant walk, a pleasant talk” (line 33). Why does he say this?
questions.explanation: The Walrus wants the Oysters to come with him, so he makes the walk sound as nice as possible. The repeated word pleasant makes it sound friendly and harmless.
options: to warn the Oysters to stay at home
to tell the Carpenter to stop crying
because he is too tired to walk far
to make the walk sound tempting so that the Oysters agree to come

questions.prompt: Compare the sun and the moon in lines 1 to 12. How are they different? Use evidence for both.
questions.explanation: The poet gives the sun and moon human feelings. They have opposite moods about the same night. Not enough on its own: descriptions of only 1 of them.
questions.misconception: Describing only 1 side of a comparison.
questions.model: The sun is trying hard and seems keen: it shines “with all his might” and “did his very best”. The moon is grumpy and annoyed, shining “sulkily” because she thinks the sun is “very rude” to be there.
checklist: The sun, with evidence: keen, hard-working or out at the wrong time (shining with all his might; did his very best; in the middle of the night).
The moon, with evidence: sulky, grumpy or annoyed (shining sulkily; It’s very rude of him; come to spoil the fun).

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of the Walrus? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the poem to support each one.
questions.explanation: Some impressions come from what the Walrus says and some from how others react to him.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
The Walrus is persuasive, because he tempts the Oysters with “A pleasant walk, a pleasant talk”. He also seems untrustworthy, since the wise eldest Oyster winks and will not “leave the oyster-bed”.

Other impressions that count:
Persuasive or charming: O Oysters, come and walk with us; a pleasant walk, a pleasant talk; did beseech
Untrustworthy or sneaky: the eldest Oyster will not go; he limits it to 4 so he can hold each by the hand
Emotional or silly: wept like anything at the sand; wants all the sand cleared away.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Working Children
units.summary: When a text gives several laws or dates, slow down. Match each year to the right change before you answer.

questions.prompt: Where was Queen Victoria born?
questions.explanation: Line 1 says Queen Victoria was born at Kensington Palace, London.

questions.prompt: Find and copy the date when Queen Victoria died.
questions.explanation: Line 2 says she reigned until she died on 22 January 1901.

questions.prompt: “the owners showed little concern for the welfare of their workers” (lines 23 to 24). What does welfare mean?
questions.explanation: Welfare means how well and safe someone is. The owners did not care much about their workers’ wellbeing.
questions.misconception: Choosing wages because the sentence is about workers and owners.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: There were only 4 inspectors (line 17), and by 1901 children were expected to go to school until the age of 12 (line 40).

statements.s: Victoria reigned for almost 64 years.
The 1842 law banned all underground work for women and girls.
The 1833 Factory Act set up a team of 40 inspectors.
By 1901, children were expected to stay at school until the age of 14.

questions.prompt: In the 1860s, Parliament gave “more than £800,000 a year towards schools” (line 29), even though no law said children had to go. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Spending so much money on schools shows Parliament already valued education, years before the 1880 law made it compulsory.
options: Parliament wanted to close the schools.
Parliament thought schools were important before school was made compulsory.
Most children were already in school.
Schools were free for every family.

questions.prompt: Match each year to the change it brought.
questions.explanation: The years are in lines 26, 30, 35 and 36. Read each sentence carefully, because some contain more than 1 year.
pairs: the age limit for boys working underground was raised to 12
school became compulsory for children aged 5 to 10
the school age was raised to 11

questions.prompt: Why do you think the 1842 report “shocked the public” (line 25)? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Lines 21 to 24 describe what the report found. Use these details to explain the public’s reaction. Not enough on its own: because it was about coal.
questions.model: The report showed that conditions in the mines “could be even worse” than in factories. Children of 8, and often younger, worked underground, girls as well as boys, and the owners cared little about their welfare.
checklist: A reason from the text: very young children worked in mines (aged 8 or younger); girls as well as boys worked; conditions were worse than in factories; owners showed little concern for their welfare.
A second reason, or for explaining why people would be shocked (they may not have known how bad it was for such young children).

questions.prompt: Which sentence best sums up lines 28 to 40?
questions.explanation: These lines describe a series of changes: school boards in 1870, compulsory school in 1880 and a rising school age, until by 1901 every child was expected to attend until 12.
options: Step by step, new laws provided schools and then made children attend them.
School was always free for every child in the 1800s.
Most children did not go to school by 1901.

questions.prompt: Dev says that the 1870 Education Act made every child go to school. Is he right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: The word finally in line 35 is a clue that compulsory school came after earlier steps such as the 1870 Act. Not enough on its own: no, with no evidence.
questions.misconception: Thinking the first law about education made school compulsory.
questions.model: No. The 1870 Act set up school boards to build and run schools in areas that needed them. It was not until 1880 that another Act “finally made school compulsory” for children aged 5 to 10.
checklist: Disagreeing with Dev and saying what the 1870 Act did: set up school boards to build and run schools.
Explaining that school only became compulsory later, in 1880 (finally made school compulsory).

questions.prompt: The text shows that passing a law was not always enough to protect children. Explain 2 reasons why, using evidence from the text.
questions.explanation: Look across both parts of the text for places where a law was passed but things did not change straight away.
questions.model:
Some laws were not checked: after the 1831 law “there was no way of making sure it was obeyed”. Even when inspectors were set up in 1833, “just 4 inspectors could not possibly keep an eye on 4,000 mills”.

Other reasons that count:
No way of checking: the 1831 law had no way of making sure it was obeyed
Too few inspectors: only 4 inspectors for 4,000 mills; the Act was widely ignored in its early years
Cost kept children away: most families still had to pay school fees until 1891
Not everyone obeyed: in the early 1890s only 82% of children were attending school.
checklist: Gives 1 reason, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different reason
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The Eagle Has Landed
units.summary: Information texts about real events often follow the order things happened. Dates and times help you keep track.

questions.prompt: On what date did Apollo 11 lift off?
questions.explanation: Line 1 says the rocket lifted off on 16 July 1969.

questions.prompt: Find and copy the name of the lunar module that landed on the Moon.
questions.explanation: Lines 7 to 8 say the lunar module was called Eagle.

questions.prompt: “unveiled a plaque” (line 24). What does unveiled mean?
questions.explanation: To unveil something is to take the cover off it so people can see it. The astronauts left a plaque on the Moon.
options: uncovered to show it for the first time

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon (lines 21 to 22), and they collected about 20 kilograms (line 25).
questions.misconception: Mixing up the 2 astronauts who landed.

statements.s: President Kennedy set the goal of landing on the Moon in 1961.
Aldrin was the first person to walk on the Moon.
The moonwalk lasted more than 2 hours.
The astronauts collected about 200 kilograms of rock and soil.

questions.prompt: “Mission Control began counting down the seconds” (line 17). What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: The sentence begins “Fuel was running low”. Counting down the seconds shows how close they were to having to give up the landing.
options: Mission Control was getting ready for lift-off.
The radio had stopped working completely.
The astronauts had very little time left before the fuel ran out.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
questions.explanation: The dates and times show the order: 16 July, 20 July, the landing at 20:17 GMT and the splashdown on 24 July.
items: Apollo 11 lifts off from Kennedy Space Center.
Armstrong and Aldrin fly down towards the Moon in Eagle.
Armstrong steers away from a rocky area.
Eagle touches down in the Sea of Tranquility.
All 3 astronauts splash down safely on Earth.

questions.prompt: Armstrong said “That’s one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind.” (lines 22 to 23). What did he mean? Explain both parts.
questions.explanation: Armstrong contrasts a tiny physical step with a huge moment in human history. Not enough on its own: he jumped a long way.
questions.misconception: Taking giant leap literally, as a big jump.
questions.model: Stepping onto the Moon was only a small step for 1 person, Armstrong himself. But it was a giant leap for mankind, because it was a huge achievement for all people on Earth.
checklist: Explaining the small step: it was just 1 ordinary step for 1 person.
Explaining the giant leap: it was a huge achievement or moment of progress for all humans.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer give exact times, such as 20:05 GMT (line 9) and 20:17 GMT (line 18)?
questions.explanation: The 2 times show the final stage of landing took about 12 to 13 minutes, which helps the reader feel how short and tense it was.
options: to show that the astronauts were late for dinner
because the times are the only facts in the text
to show how long the tense landing took and to record exactly when it happened
to tell the reader what time it is now

questions.prompt: Ruby says the Moon landing went exactly to plan. Is she right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Lines 11 to 18 describe several problems. The landing succeeded, but not in the way it was planned. Not enough on its own: no, with no evidence.
questions.misconception: Assuming that a successful mission had no problems.
questions.model: No. During the landing the radio signal kept dropping out and alarms flashed up on the computer. The computer was also guiding Eagle towards “a rocky area near a crater”, so Armstrong had to take control, and fuel was running low.
checklist: Disagreeing with Ruby.
Evidence of a problem: the radio kept dropping out; unfamiliar alarms (1202 and 1201); the computer guided them towards a rocky area; Armstrong had to take control; fuel was running low.

questions.prompt: How does the text show that Apollo 11 was a success? Give 2 points, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Look back at the aim in lines 2 to 3 and check how much of it was achieved by the end.
questions.model:
Apollo 11 achieved its main aim, which was “to land people on the Moon and return them safely to Earth”: they landed, and on 24 July “all 3 splashed down safely”. Armstrong also became “the first person to walk on the Moon”.

Other points that count:
Achieved its aim: landed people on the Moon and returned them safely; all 3 splashed down safely on 24 July
A first in history: Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon
Work done on the Moon: put up a flag and scientific instruments; unveiled a plaque; collected about 20 kilograms of rock and soil
Problems overcome: alarms, radio drop-outs and a rocky site were dealt with and Eagle landed.
checklist: Gives 1 point, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different point
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: South
units.summary: In a true account, the writer’s word choices show how they felt. Look for comparisons and strong verbs that make events vivid.

questions.prompt: How many emperor penguins suddenly appeared?
questions.explanation: Line 19 describes the sudden appearance of “eight emperor penguins”.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 25 to 27. Find and copy the words that tell you what could be seen from the crow’s-nest.
questions.explanation: Lines 26 to 27 say that from the crow’s-nest there was no sign of land of any sort.
questions.answer: no sign of land of any sort

questions.prompt: “the faint, indefinable whispers of our ship’s distress” (lines 6 to 7). What does indefinable mean?
questions.explanation: Something indefinable cannot be clearly described. Shackleton could hear quiet noises from the ship but could not say exactly what they were.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: Men and dogs went down to the floe together (line 39), and the camp was moved to a floe about 200 yds away (line 49).

statements.s: All hands were pumping all night.
The ice split the rudder.
The dogs were left behind on the ship.
The camp was moved to a bigger floe about 500 yds away.

questions.prompt: “It was a sickening sensation” (line 34). What does this show about how Shackleton felt?
questions.explanation: The sentence goes on to describe the decks breaking up under his feet. Sickening shows the horror of feeling the ship being destroyed.
questions.misconception: Reading sickening as being physically ill.
options: He was excited to start camping on the ice.
He was seasick from the waves.
He was horrified and upset to feel his ship breaking apart.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
questions.explanation: Use the times: 4 p.m., 5 p.m., just before leaving, the camp for the night, and the move at about 7 p.m.
items: The ice splits the rudder and tears out the stern-post.
Shackleton orders all hands on to the ice.
He sees the engines dropping sideways.
A camp is made about 100 yds from the ship.
The camp is moved to a bigger floe.

questions.prompt: Why did a pioneer party have to build a snow-causeway (lines 53 to 54)? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Lines 51 to 55 explain the problem and the solution. Use both parts in your answer. Not enough on its own: to stop the ship from sinking.
questions.model: The weight of the pressure-ridge had made the floes sink on either side, leaving pools of water. The men needed a raised path so they could get the boats, stores and camp equipment across to the new floe.
checklist: The cause: the weight of the ridge made the floes sink, leaving pools of water.
The purpose: they needed a path to carry their possessions (boats, stores, equipment) across to the new camp.

questions.prompt: “the great beams bending and then snapping with a noise like heavy gunfire” (lines 35 to 36). What effect does this comparison have?
questions.explanation: Heavy gunfire is loud, sudden and frightening. The comparison makes the reader hear the ship being torn apart.
options: It shows the ship was quiet and calm.
It shows the crew were firing guns at the ice.
It shows how loud and violent the destruction of the ship was.
It shows the beams were made of metal.

questions.prompt: Lines 25 to 45 come from the diary Shackleton wrote on the day the ship was lost. Why do you think he included his diary at this point? Explain your answer.
questions.explanation: A diary is written on the day. Including it brings the reader right into the most important moment of the account. Not enough on its own: because he forgot what happened.
questions.model: Including the diary lets the reader hear exactly what Shackleton thought and felt on that day, as it was happening. Words such as “our last on the ship” and “a sickening sensation” make the moment feel real and close.
checklist: Explaining that the diary shows his thoughts and feelings at the time, as it happened.
The effect on the reader: it makes the event feel real, vivid or immediate; it shows it is a true account; with a reference such as our last on the ship or a sickening sensation.

questions.prompt: How does Shackleton make the ice seem like a powerful enemy? Give 2 ways, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Shackleton uses the language of war and battle. Collect words that make the ice sound like an army attacking the ship.
questions.model:
He describes the ice as if it were attacking: “The attack of the ice reached its climax”. He also shows its enormous strength, with “Millions of tons of ice” pressing on “the little ship”.

Other ways that count:
The ice attacks or fights: the attack of the ice; a one-sided battle; the floes working their will at last
Huge size and strength: millions of tons of ice; pressed inexorably; titanic pressure
Destruction: split the rudder; tore out the rudder-post and stern-post; simply annihilating the ship
The ship is small and brave by comparison: the little ship that had dared the challenge; she resisted like a living creature.
checklist: Gives 1 way, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different way
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin
units.summary: Poets choose sounds as well as meanings. When you explain an effect, say what the words make you picture or hear.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the river the rats came to?
questions.explanation: Line 24 says they came to the river Weser.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 1 to 4. Find and copy the words that tell you how the Piper smiled.
questions.explanation: Line 2 says he stepped into the street “Smiling first a little smile”.

questions.prompt: “And ere three shrill notes the pipe uttered” (line 9). What does shrill mean?
questions.explanation: A shrill sound is high and sharp. The Piper’s notes are loud enough to be heard all over the town.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the poem is true or false.
questions.explanation: The rats “followed dancing” (line 23), and the Piper led them to the river Weser, not the sea (line 24).

statements.s: Only 1 rat survived.
The rats walked slowly and sadly behind the Piper.
The rats came tumbling out of the houses.
The Piper led the rats to the sea.

questions.prompt: “Families by tens and dozens” (line 19). What does this line tell you?
questions.explanation: Tens and dozens of whole families shows that the rats came out in enormous numbers.
options: There were only a few rats.
The rats were counting as they walked.
There were huge numbers of rats.
The rats lived on their own.

questions.prompt: Put these events from the poem in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The poem follows the Piper from the street (line 1) to the river (lines 24 to 25).
items: The Piper steps into the street and smiles.
He blows his pipe.
The rats come tumbling out of the houses.
The rats follow him dancing from street to street.
The rats plunge into the river Weser.

questions.prompt: The Piper smiles “As if he knew what magic slept” (line 3) in his pipe. What does this suggest about the Piper? Explain using the poem.
questions.explanation: The word slept suggests the magic is waiting, ready to wake up. The Piper smiles because he knows what is coming. Not enough on its own: he is nervous.
questions.model: It suggests the Piper is confident, because he already knows his pipe has a magic power that will work. His “little smile” before he plays shows he is calm and sure of what will happen.
checklist: An impression: confident, sure of himself, knowing, mysterious or magical.
Explaining with the poem: he smiles before he plays; he knows the magic is waiting in his pipe; the pipe is quiet but powerful.

questions.prompt: “Like a candle-flame where salt is sprinkled” (line 8). What does this comparison suggest about the Piper’s eyes?
questions.explanation: Sprinkling salt on a flame makes it spark and flicker. The Piper’s green and blue eyes twinkle in a strange, magical way.
questions.misconception: Thinking the comparison is about salt or candles themselves rather than the way his eyes look.
options: They sparkled and flickered with strange, bright colours.
They were closed while he played.

questions.prompt: Lines 14 to 20 are a long list of different kinds of rats. Why do you think the poet uses such a long list? Explain using the poem.
questions.explanation: Lists can do more than give information. Here the length and rhythm of the list help the reader picture the crowd of rats. Not enough on its own: to tell us the colours of rats, with no explanation.
questions.model: The long list shows that every kind of rat came out: “Great rats, small rats, lean rats, brawny rats”. It goes on and on, just like the endless stream of rats pouring out of the houses, and the bouncy rhythm sounds like them scurrying.
checklist: Explaining that it shows there were huge numbers or every kind of rat.
The effect of the list itself: it seems to go on and on like the stream of rats; or it creates a fast, bouncy rhythm like scurrying feet; with a reference to the list.

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of the Piper? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the poem to support each one.
questions.explanation: The Piper says nothing at all in this part of the poem, so your impressions must come from how he looks and what his music does.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
The Piper is confident, because he smiles “As if he knew what magic slept” in his pipe. He is also very powerful, since all the rats “Followed the Piper for their lives” and then “all plunged and perished”.

Other impressions that count:
Confident or calm: smiling first a little smile; as if he knew what magic slept
Mysterious or magical: green and blue eyes that twinkled like a candle-flame with salt; magic in his pipe
Skilled: like a musical adept
Powerful: the rats come tumbling out and follow him for their lives; he leads them all into the river.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: The War of the Worlds
units.summary: Writers build fear slowly. Notice how the description moves from what the narrator can hardly see to what he sees clearly.

questions.prompt: What did the narrator hear coming from the pit?
questions.explanation: Line 7 says he heard a peculiar humming sound from the pit.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 12 to 15. Find and copy the word that tells you what the lid of the cylinder fell on.
questions.explanation: Line 15 says the lid fell upon the gravel with a ringing concussion.

questions.prompt: “the lipless brim of which quivered and panted” (line 36). What does quivered mean?
questions.explanation: To quiver is to shake or tremble a little. The Martian’s mouth is never still.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: The narrator began pushing his way back from the edge (line 26), and the creature rose “slowly and painfully” (line 32).

statements.s: The narrator had the sunset in his eyes.
Stent was among the people who ran off.
The narrator ran towards the pit when the creature appeared.
The first creature rose quickly and easily out of the cylinder.

questions.prompt: “I ran slantingly and stumbling, for I could not avert my face from these things” (line 54). Why did the narrator run like this?
questions.explanation: Avert means turn away. He kept looking back as he ran, so he moved sideways and stumbled.
options: He was injured in the crowd.
The ground was covered in ice.
He could not stop looking back at the creatures.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the Martian to how it is described.
questions.explanation: The descriptions are in lines 33, 34, 40 and 46.
pairs: V-shaped with a pointed upper lip

questions.prompt: The creature moved with “evident heaviness and painfulness” (line 43). Why did it move like this? What does this tell you about where it came from?
questions.explanation: Lines 43 to 44 give the cause. Working out what that means about the Martian’s home is the inference. Not enough on its own: it was old or injured, with no link to gravity.
questions.model: The text says this was “due to the greater gravitational energy of the earth”. The pull of gravity on Earth is stronger than the creature is used to, which suggests it has come from another planet with weaker gravity, Mars.
checklist: The reason in the text: the earth’s greater gravitational energy (gravity) made it heavy and painful to move.
The inference: it comes from somewhere with weaker gravity, another planet, Mars (it is called a Martian).

questions.prompt: “greyish billowy movements, one above another” (line 20). Why does the writer describe the creature so vaguely at first?
questions.explanation: The narrator sees “something stirring within the shadow” (line 20). Giving only shapes and movements keeps the reader guessing, like the crowd.
options: It is in shadow and he cannot see it clearly yet, which builds suspense.
He has forgotten what it looked like.
He is not interested in the creature.

questions.prompt: Kai thinks the narrator was brave because he stayed by the pit when other people ran off. Is Kai right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Petrified means so frightened you cannot move. Staying still was not a choice the narrator made. Not enough on its own: yes, because he stayed.
questions.misconception: Judging a character by an action without checking the reason the text gives.
questions.model: No. The narrator did not stay because he was brave. He says “ungovernable terror gripped me” and “I stood petrified”, which means he was too frightened to move. When he could move, he ran “madly” to the trees.
checklist: Disagreeing: he stayed because he was frozen with fear, not because he was brave.
Evidence: ungovernable terror gripped me; I stood petrified and staring; a sudden chill; running madly.

questions.prompt: How do the narrator’s feelings change during the text? Give 2 different feelings, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Track the narrator through the text: before the lid opens, when he sees the tentacles, and after he sees the Martian clearly.
questions.model:
At first the narrator is curious and excited: he “elbowed my way through” the crowd to see. Later he is terrified, as “ungovernable terror gripped me”, and he is “overcome with disgust and dread” when he sees the Martian.

Other feelings that count:
Curious or excited at first: elbowed his way through; every one seemed greatly excited; he expected to see a man
Frightened or terrified: a sudden chill came over me; ungovernable terror; petrified; running madly
Disgusted: overcome with disgust and dread; unspeakably nasty
Fascinated as well as afraid: could not avert his face; half-fascinated terror.
checklist: Gives 1 feeling, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different feeling
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Into the Deep
units.summary: Information texts often give several numbers close together. Check which number answers the exact question before you choose.

questions.prompt: What is the depth of the deepest place in the ocean?
questions.explanation: Line 3 says the Challenger Deep is about 10,935 metres deep. 3,682 metres is the average depth of the whole ocean.
questions.misconception: Choosing the first number in the text (the average depth) instead of the one the question asks for.

questions.prompt: Find and copy the name of the creature that roams the deep seafloor eating dead fish.
questions.explanation: Lines 26 to 27 say the giant isopod roams the deep seafloor, feasting on dead fish.

questions.prompt: “Light may be detected as far as 1,000 metres” (line 4). What does detected mean?
questions.explanation: To detect something is to notice or discover it. A tiny amount of light can still be found 1,000 metres down.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: In the twilight zone the light fades too fast for plants to use it (lines 7 to 8). In some anglerfish the males are tiny (line 25).

statements.s: Plants can use the light in the twilight zone to make food.
There are over 200 kinds of deep-sea anglerfish.
A whale’s ribs are joined by loose, bendable cartilage.
In some kinds of anglerfish, the males are much bigger than the females.

questions.prompt: A whale’s rib cage can fold in “at pressures that would snap our bones” (line 20). What does this suggest about humans?
questions.explanation: Our ribs are not flexible like a whale’s, so the pressure in the deep would break them. We could not go there without special protection.
options: Humans could not survive the deep ocean without protection.
Humans do not feel pressure at all.
Humans can dive deeper than whales.
Humans have stronger bones than whales.

questions.prompt: Put these topics in the order the text covers them.
questions.explanation: The text starts with depth (lines 1 to 3), moves to light (lines 4 to 11) and pressure (lines 12 to 17), then to the animals (lines 18 to 27).
items: how deep the ocean is
how sunlight fades and the zones it creates
how water pressure increases
how whales cope with pressure
how anglerfish catch food

questions.prompt: Explain why whales can survive great changes in pressure. Use the text in your answer.
questions.explanation: Lines 18 to 20 give both parts of the answer: what is special about whale ribs and why that helps. Not enough on its own: because whales are very big.
questions.misconception: Giving a general reason (size) that the text does not mention.
questions.model: Whales have flexible bodies. Their ribs are “joined by loose, bendable cartilage”, so the rib cage can fold in under great pressure instead of snapping.
checklist: Saying their bodies are flexible or their ribs are joined by loose, bendable cartilage.
Explaining the result: the rib cage folds in rather than breaking or snapping under pressure.

questions.prompt: “This dark world includes the midnight zone” (line 9). Why does the writer call the deep ocean a world?
questions.explanation: Calling the deep sea a world suggests it is like a whole other place, with darkness, pressure and strange animals unlike anything on land.
options: because it is a separate planet
because it is shown on world maps
because it is a huge place with its own conditions and creatures, very different from ours
because whales travel around the world

questions.prompt: Leo says the giant isopod hunts for its food in the same way as the anglerfish. Is he right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: The word Other in line 26 signals a different way of finding food. Scavenging and luring prey are not the same. Not enough on its own: no, with no explanation of how they differ.
questions.misconception: Thinking every deep-sea animal hunts live prey.
questions.model: No. The giant isopod is a scavenger: it eats “dead fish and other scraps that drift down from above”. The anglerfish catches living prey by luring it with a glowing light into her mouth.
checklist: The isopod: it scavenges, eating dead fish and scraps that drift down.
The anglerfish: it catches living prey using a glowing lure.

questions.prompt: How does the text show that some creatures are well suited to life in the deep ocean? Give 2 examples, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: For each creature, say what the problem is (pressure, darkness or lack of food) and how the creature deals with it.
questions.model:
Whales cope with the pressure because “their bodies are flexible”. Anglerfish can catch food in the dark because the female has a glowing lure that prey swim towards.

Other examples that count:
Whales: flexible bodies; ribs joined by bendable cartilage; the rib cage folds in instead of snapping
Anglerfish: a glowing lure full of light-producing bacteria attracts prey in the dark
Giant isopod: scavenges dead fish and scraps, so it can feed where food is hard to find.
checklist: Gives 1 example, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different example
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Sutton Hoo
units.summary: Information texts often say how sure experts are. Watch for words such as suggests, probably and theory, which show something is not certain.

questions.prompt: How long was the ship found at Sutton Hoo?
questions.explanation: Line 9 says the ship was 27 metres long.

questions.prompt: Find and copy the name of the man who made the discovery in 1939.
questions.explanation: Line 6 says a man called Basil Brown made the discovery.

questions.prompt: “revealed the shape of a ship” (lines 8 to 9). What does revealed mean?
questions.explanation: As the archaeologists brushed away the soil, the shape of the ship was uncovered for people to see.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: The timbers had rotted away, leaving only an imprint (lines 9 to 10). The garnets most likely came from Sri Lanka (lines 36 to 37).

statements.s: Sutton Hoo is in the east of England.
The ship’s wooden timbers were found in perfect condition.
The helmet was crushed into more than 100 pieces.
The red garnets most likely came from Egypt.

questions.prompt: A time that had “often been seen as backward” (line 16) was shown to be cultured. What does this tell you about the discovery?
questions.explanation: Line 15 says the find changed what people thought. The treasures showed skill and wealth, so the old idea of a backward people was wrong.
options: It showed the Anglo-Saxons had no treasure.
It changed what people thought about the Anglo-Saxons.
It proved the Anglo-Saxons were not very clever.

questions.prompt: Match each object to what the text says it suggests or shows.
questions.explanation: Lines 24 to 25 and lines 34 to 35 explain what each object tells us about the person buried.
pairs: modelled on those worn by Roman emperors

questions.prompt: Experts think the shield may have been “a diplomatic gift from Scandinavia” (line 33). What does this suggest about the king who was buried? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: The text explains what a diplomatic gift is (lines 33 to 34). Ask yourself what kind of person receives presents from other rulers. Not enough on its own: he went to Scandinavia to buy a shield.
questions.model: A diplomatic gift is “a present sent from one ruler to another”. If another ruler sent him a gift, the king must have been important and had friendly links with powerful people in other lands.
checklist: An inference: the king was important, respected or powerful.
Explaining why: rulers in other lands sent him gifts; he had friendly links with Scandinavia; with reference to a present sent from one ruler to another.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best sums up lines 17 to 22?
questions.explanation: These lines describe the public burial and explain that ship burial belonged to the time before the Anglo-Saxons became Christian. After that, burials changed enormously.
options: The ship was found by accident in a river.
Anglo-Saxons always buried their dead in ships.
A whole community buried their king in a ship, a custom from before they became Christian.

questions.prompt: Grace says we know for certain that the king buried at Sutton Hoo was Rædwald. Is she right? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: A theory is the best explanation experts have, not a proven fact. Lines 44 to 46 make this clear. Not enough on its own: no, with no evidence.
questions.misconception: Treating a theory as a proven fact.
questions.model: No. The text says “We will never know for certain who was buried there”. Rædwald is only “the leading theory”, because the coins date the burial to around 625 and he died around this time.
checklist: Disagreeing with Grace, using the text: we will never know for certain; it is only the leading theory.
Explaining why experts think it might be Rædwald: the coins suggest about 625, and he died around this time.

questions.prompt: How does the text show that the work of the archaeologists at Sutton Hoo was careful and difficult? Give 2 points, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Look across both parts of the text for the different stages of the work: digging, rebuilding and testing.
questions.model:
The archaeologists “carefully brushed away layers of sandy soil” to find a ship that was only “a ghostly imprint in the sand”. Rebuilding the helmet was hard too: it was in more than 100 pieces and “took experts at the British Museum many years”.

Other points that count:
Careful digging: carefully brushed away layers of sandy soil; the timbers had rotted, leaving only a ghostly imprint
Rebuilding: the helmet was crushed into more than 100 pieces and took many years to rebuild
Scientific testing: they returned between 1965 and 1971; tests on the sand found phosphate, showing a body had been there
Some answers can never be found: the acidic soil dissolved the body; we will never know for certain who was buried.
checklist: Gives 1 point, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different point
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: Goblin Market
units.summary: In a poem with 2 characters, compare what each one says and does. Their actions are often the clearest evidence.

questions.prompt: What were the goblins selling?
questions.explanation: The goblins cry “Come buy our orchard fruits” (line 3), then list many kinds of fruit.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 56 to 59. Find and copy the words that tell you what 1 of the goblins lugs.
questions.explanation: Line 58 says “One lugs a golden dish”.
accept: a golden dish of many pounds’ weight

questions.prompt: “Whose grapes are so luscious” (line 61). What does luscious mean?
questions.explanation: Luscious means very juicy and tasty. Laura imagines how wonderful the goblins’ grapes must be.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the poem is true or false.
questions.explanation: It was Lizzie who covered her eyes (line 50). The goblins were hobbling down the glen (line 47).
questions.misconception: Mixing up the 2 sisters.

statements.s: Laura and Lizzie crouched close together among the rushes.
Laura covered up her eyes so she would not see the goblins.
Lizzie put a finger in each ear and ran.
The goblins were hobbling up a mountain.

questions.prompt: Laura “whispered like the restless brook” (line 53). What does restless suggest about Laura?
questions.explanation: A restless brook never stops moving. Laura is excited and cannot stop herself watching the goblins.
options: She cannot keep still because she is eager to look.
She is tired and wants to sleep.

questions.prompt: Put these events from the poem in the order they happen.
questions.explanation: The cry fills lines 1 to 31. The sisters appear from line 32, and Lizzie runs away in line 68.
items: The goblins call out the names of their fruits.
Laura and Lizzie crouch together by the brook.
Laura says they must not look at goblin men.
Laura describes the little men coming down the glen.
Lizzie puts her fingers in her ears and runs.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 40 to 45 and lines 52 to 63. How does Laura change? Use evidence from both parts.
questions.explanation: Laura says one thing and then does the opposite. The change shows how tempting the goblins are. Not enough on its own: answers that describe only 1 part.
questions.misconception: Describing only 1 side of a change.
questions.model: At first Laura warns her sister: “We must not look at goblin men”. Later she does look, and she even admires the fruit, saying “How fair the vine must grow”.
checklist: The first part, with evidence: Laura is careful or warns against the goblins (We must not look at goblin men; We must not buy their fruits).
The second part, with evidence: Laura looks and is tempted (reared her glossy head; Look, Lizzie, look; How fair the vine must grow; grapes so luscious).

questions.prompt: The goblins repeat “Come buy, come buy” (line 4) again and again. What is the effect of this repetition?
questions.explanation: The repeated call sounds like a market cry that never stops, which makes the goblins hard to ignore.
options: It shows that the fruit is cheap.
It makes the poem feel sad and slow.
It sounds like market sellers calling over and over, tempting people to buy.
It shows the goblins have forgotten what to say.

questions.prompt: The poem begins with 31 lines of the goblins’ cry before we meet Laura and Lizzie. Why do you think the poet organised the poem like this? Explain your answer.
questions.explanation: The order of a poem matters. Starting with the cry puts the temptation in the reader’s ears before the sisters respond to it. Not enough on its own: because the goblins are the main characters, with no explanation.
questions.model: The reader hears the long, tempting cry first, just as the sisters do “Morning and evening”. By the time Laura and Lizzie appear, we already understand how tempting the fruit is, so we can see why Laura finds it hard to resist.
checklist: Explaining that the reader hears the cry first, like the sisters do, or that it shows how tempting the goblins’ fruit is.
The effect: it prepares the reader for the sisters’ reactions, or helps us understand why Laura is tempted.

questions.prompt: What impressions do you get of the goblins? Give 2 impressions, using evidence from the poem to support each one.
questions.explanation: The goblins speak in the first part, and the sisters react to them in the second. Use both for evidence.
questions.misconception: Giving an impression without any evidence.
questions.model:
The goblins are tempting, because they call out a long list of delicious fruits such as “Plump unpecked cherries”. They may also be dangerous: Lizzie warns that “Their evil gifts would harm us”.

Other impressions that count:
Tempting or persuasive: the long list of fruit; Come buy, come buy; Taste them and try
Dangerous or evil: Their evil gifts would harm us; Laura wonders what soil fed their roots; Lizzie runs away
Strange or creepy: hobbling down the glen; little men
Rich: a golden dish of many pounds’ weight.
checklist: Gives 1 impression, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different impression
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)

units.title: A Christmas Carol
units.summary: Dickens often describes a character through comparisons. When you explain one, say what the 2 things have in common.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 25 to 26. On what day does this part of the story take place?
questions.explanation: Line 25 says it was Christmas Eve.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 40 to 41. Find and copy the words that tell you what the clerk put on to try to keep warm.
questions.explanation: Line 40 says the clerk put on his white comforter, a long woollen scarf.

questions.prompt: “No beggars implored him to bestow a trifle” (lines 16 to 17). What does implored mean?
questions.explanation: To implore is to beg. Beggars did not even bother to ask Scrooge for money.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the text is true or false.
questions.explanation: The nephew had been rapid walking (line 46), and Scrooge “didn’t thaw it one degree at Christmas” (line 8).

statements.s: Scrooge kept the coal-box in his own room.
Scrooge’s nephew arrived slowly in a carriage.
The fog was so thick that the houses opposite looked like phantoms.
Scrooge’s office became warmer at Christmas.

questions.prompt: “Nobody ever stopped him in the street” (line 15) to ask how he was. What does this tell you about how people felt about Scrooge?
questions.explanation: Nobody greets him, asks him for help or even asks the time. People keep away from him because he is so cold and mean.
options: They did not know who he was.
They were waiting for him to speak first.
They were too busy to talk to anyone.
They avoided him because he was so unfriendly.

questions.prompt: Match each thing to how Dickens describes it.
questions.explanation: The descriptions are in line 2, lines 30 to 31, line 33 and line 37.
pairs: ruddy smears upon the palpable brown air
so very much smaller that it looked like one coal

questions.prompt: Scrooge asks his nephew “What right have you to be merry?” (line 50) and says “You’re poor enough.” (line 51). What does this show about what Scrooge believes? Explain using the text.
questions.explanation: Scrooge links being merry with being rich. His nephew’s reply in lines 52 to 53 shows how wrong that idea is. Not enough on its own: scrooge thinks his nephew is rich.
questions.misconception: Missing the link Scrooge makes between money and happiness.
questions.model: It shows Scrooge believes that only money gives people a reason to be happy. Because his nephew is poor, Scrooge thinks he has no right to enjoy Christmas.
checklist: The belief: happiness depends on money, or poor people have no reason to be happy.
Linking this to the text: he says the nephew is poor enough, so he has no right or reason to be merry.

questions.prompt: The nephew replies “What right have you to be dismal?” (line 52). Why is this a clever answer?
questions.explanation: The nephew copies the pattern of Scrooge’s questions but swaps merry for dismal and poor for rich. Scrooge has no answer except “Bah!”.
options: He agrees with everything Scrooge says.
He asks Scrooge to lend him money.
He changes the subject to the weather.
He turns Scrooge’s own words back on him, showing that being rich does not make Scrooge happy.

questions.prompt: Do you think Scrooge will change his mind about Christmas? Use evidence from the text to support your prediction.
questions.explanation: Either prediction can be right. What matters is the evidence you give from the text. Not enough on its own: a prediction with no link to the text.
questions.model: I think he might change later, because when his nephew argues back Scrooge has “no better answer ready”, which suggests his argument is weak. For now, though, he only says “Bah!” and “Humbug”, so any change will not happen easily.
checklist: A clear prediction (Yes, No, or not easily).

Evidence: Yes, because he has no better answer ready, or his nephew is cheerful and keeps trying; No, because he says Bah! Humbug! twice, likes being avoided, and keeps his office icy even at Christmas.

questions.prompt: How does the writer show that Scrooge is mean to his clerk? Give 2 points, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.explanation: Lines 35 to 41 show how Scrooge treats the clerk. Pick 2 different points rather than 2 examples of the same thing.
questions.misconception: Giving 2 examples of the same point instead of 2 different points.
questions.model:
Scrooge keeps the clerk cold: the clerk’s fire is so small “that it looked like one coal”, and Scrooge keeps the coal-box in his own room. He also watches him, leaving the door open “that he might keep his eye upon his clerk”.

Other points that count:
Keeps him cold: tiny fire like one coal; Scrooge keeps the coal-box; the clerk has to warm himself at the candle
Threatens him: if the clerk comes for coal, Scrooge says it would be necessary for them to part
Watches him: the door is open so Scrooge can keep his eye on him
Gives him a poor place to work: a dismal little cell, a sort of tank.
checklist: Gives 1 point, linked to the text
Gives a 2nd, different point
Backs up at least 1 of them with evidence (a quotation or a detail from the text)
